title.rendered: AI Asks Its Humans: “Where’s My Flux Capacitor?”

content.rendered:
Podcast: Play in new window

The AI boom is making enormous promises. But can the power supply, infrastructure, and revenues keep up with the debt being used to finance it? This week, David McAlvany examines the risks behind a projected $10 trillion AI buildout, from construction delays and rapidly outdated chips to revenue assumptions that leave little room for error. As AI debt spreads through banks, pension funds, and global bond markets, could a bust create a crisis bigger than 2008?

  • Powering AI: 143 Hoover Dams or 301 Nuclear Power Plants
  • AI Debt Could Fuel the Biggest Bubble in History

  • Recommended Reading: “Financing the AI Buildout” by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, Columbia Business School

“We have to wonder at the sanity of private capital sprinting towards the infinite money tree of AI, and you also have to wonder at the prudence of lending money to governments over any meaningful period of time—two, three, five, 10 years—when they have no plan to pay it back at its original value. Pay it back with interest, but what about the devaluation piece? The debasement trade is not a quarter opportunity. It’s probably an accelerating quarter-century reality that affects the global middle class in a way that I think you could describe as a reset.” —David McAlvany

*     *     *

Kevin: Welcome to the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. I’m Kevin Orrick along with David McAlvany.

David, we’ve been talking a lot about AI and the financing for AI. A lot of people want to focus on what it does for them or what it doesn’t do for them, but actually we’re talking trillions of dollars, billions of dollars, we’re talking gigawatts, and I think we need to put some things into perspective. What’s a gigawatt?

David: Well, that’s a great question. We need to ask Doc Brown from Back to the Future. That and the flux capacitor will get you back to the future.

Kevin: That’s what—

David: You need 1.21 gigawatts.

Kevin: The DeLorean, right?

David: That’s right.

Kevin: 1.21 gigawatts.

David: A nuclear facility typically has about gigawatt power, generates that amount of power.

Kevin: Okay. And Hoover Dam?

David: Just over two.

Kevin: Okay. And so what we’re talking about, that’s obviously a lot of power and a lot of electron volts. I can at least use that one. But as we talk through these things today, because you and I have been talking about AI, I think it’s good to keep that in perspective. We know what a billion is. It’s hard for us to get our head around what a trillion dollars is, but we’re going to be talking those numbers right now, and there certainly is an awful lot expected of AI in the gigawatt area and in the billions and trillions areas. So let’s go ahead and get started with that.

David: Well, the last time we looked at AI was with a guest, and circular financing, some shady Cayman structures, the sustainability of debt in the sector. Those were all topics we discussed. And if you missed it, I would go back and give it a listen.

I’m linking a paper by a Columbia professor. He’s a business school professor there, and that’ll be in the show notes today. If you are an AI enthusiast, if you’re an AI skeptic, if— Maybe you’re just concerned about the Anthropic disclosures for their IPO, offering up that there’s as much as a 10% chance that AI, their technology, annihilates the human race. That’s a risk disclosure worth paying attention to. I don’t think that’s ever been put into an IPO disclosure, risk disclosure doc. But this paper from the Columbia professor, it takes hypothetical risks and conservatively addresses the math of the build-out. It’s about the math and whether it works or not.

Kevin: Well, and when we talk about build-out, America’s had some major costs in the past, so Panama Canal, the railroads, and I don’t know that there’s ever been a 10% chance of annihilation of the human race, though, like with the railroads or the Panama Canal, even if it didn’t work. So let’s go ahead and talk about the cost perspective. Let’s take that and let’s go back and let’s look at the electrical build-out.

David: Well, in short, I mean, this is a boom that has no equal in US financial market history. And to not bust, everything has to go just right, from financing to timing to sequencing of scarce resources and getting the projects delivered on time and as close to budget as possible.

Kevin: So if everything runs perfectly, this might just work.

David: In a perfect world, it’s possible, and I think that’s what the Trump administration is leaning into. Let’s not get off the path towards a perfect world. In the world we inhabit, the probabilities are low, and I was left to conclude that this boom is setting up for a bust far greater than the global financial crisis.

When you look at the interlinkages throughout the global economy connected to AI, they’re growing, and with it the multiplication of vulnerabilities. So the markets at risk include the equity markets of course, the bond markets, private credit, insurance, pension funds, commercial banking, a lot of lending through commercial banks as well.

So the scale dwarfs the mortgage-backed securities and asset-backed securities alchemy of ’05 to ’07. And the risks discussed in this paper, again, we’re going to link that at the bottom of the show notes, they’re not what Rickards discussed with us a month or so ago, or our most recent guest—again, focusing on one primary aspect of dysfunction: circular financing. The paper is— And it’s not a postmortem either. If you wanted to understand in advance what missed the mark, this I think is something of a cheat sheet, and you have it laid out prior to the bursting of the bubble. I think it brings a lot of insight.

Kevin: You said it’s about a 27-page paper, but well worth reading.

David: 29. Brookings— Well, anyways, it’ll be at the bottom. So this is the largest infrastructure investment in US history. It exceeds the build-out of the US canal system, 1836 to 1841, the railroad expansion from 1870 to 1890, and the electrification of the country, which was a 20-year span, 1905 to 1925. Telecom boom went from ’96 to ’03, and that laid the fiber needed for our current internet age. And in each of the cases, I mean, this author takes the current dollar investment—current at that time—current dollar investment, divides it by nominal GDP, also in that time frame.

Kevin: So that gives us an idea of what it costs. That’s what we were starting the show with. Let’s go ahead and get our head around it. What did these projects cost in GDP?

David: The canal system averaged 66 basis points, 66.66 of a percent of GDP annually, and it peaked at 0.9%.

Kevin: And at that point, that was the largest infrastructure investment that the US had made.

David: Yep. Then the rail system blew it away. It averaged 2.2% of GDP, with the peak hitting 4% in two years, 1870 and 1881. And that was—

Kevin: And we’re beneficiaries of that because we live in Durango, Colorado. The railroad came right out here.

David: And we also talked about the fact that at that point there were very few listed companies, and the concentration—the capitalization of stocks in the railroad sector—was 60% of total stock market capitalization at that time. If you look at every other boom, the max has gotten to about 40%, which is what we’re up to—within a few percentage points of reaching—now. So that was the extraordinary situation in terms of market cap-to-GDP.

Electrification averaged half a percent per year, peaking in 1924 at 96 basis points, just under 1%. The highway investment—and again, this is this massive, massive investment—averaged 1.13% of GDP per year. It peaked in 1958 at 1.32%. Telecoms averaged 1.1% of GDP and peaked in the year 2000 at 1.39%. Again, these were sort of massive booms.

The AI build-out, by contrast, I mean this accounts for an expansion of gigawatts—I didn’t say jigawatts.

Kevin: Like they did in Back to the Future.

David: We’ll leave Doc Brown in the past.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: Yeah, the expansion of gigawatt usage and data centers from the end of the year 2024, which was 39 gigawatts, to a total of 566 gigawatts by 2032.

Kevin: Wow.

David: And then the author’s assumptions include an estimate of 226 of those gigawatts out of the 566 being canceled or downsized for a variety of reasons. So—

Kevin: So he’s trying to play it conservative. He’s not saying it’s running perfect.

David: 566 is the stated goal, and we’re not going to get there. So he’s adjusted everything down to much more reasonable expectations, and he’s got tons of math as you would expect a professor to have.

Kevin: Right.

David: So the remaining projects being brought online tally in cost to $10.3 trillion, and that’s from 2025 through 2032. 10.3 trillion. The average annual investment as a percentage of GDP, 3.6%—3.63.

Kevin: So of all those that we’ve been comparing to, that’s the highest so far.

David: Yeah. 2026, 4.5% in the paper. 2027, 4.2%. The final year, 2032 gobbles at 5.1% of GDP.

Kevin: Wow.

David: So keep in mind nominal US GDP last year, 2025, 30.76 trillion, and 2032, GDP is estimated to be over 40, about 40 and a half, 40.5.

Kevin: Okay. So we’re talking a lot of money right now, but we’re not talking money that’s actually being earned. What we’re talking about is money that has to be borrowed, right? I mean, how much is actually coming out of profits?

David: Well, again, that’s a great contrast because in the early days, hyperscalers took their free cash flow winnings, hundreds of billions on balance sheet from their other revenue sources, and they recycled them into the data center investments. But the sums anticipated, again, totaling 10.3 trillion, they exceed the hyperscaler cash flow. So again, we’re talking about Amazon, we’re talking about Microsoft, Meta, the big ones.

Kevin: They can’t afford it. And so they’re going to go borrow it.

David: They have to tap the debt markets. That’s what they’ve been doing. And here’s the problem. The biggest problem as I see it is execution risk, even as interest payments are accruing. So on-time completion of the data centers, that can generate cash inflows—again, generating revenue. They have to match the cash outflows to service the debt. So project completions are really critical. The problem is, they also have a number of impediments: permitting, land development, sourcing electricity, those interconnectivities with the utilities, dealing with supply chain constraints for turbines and cooling equipment and chips. Even within the delivery of chips, once created, the chips have to be packaged. They have to be encapsulated prior to use, which requires them to be shipped overseas and then back again, and—

Kevin: That sounds trivial, doesn’t it? That the packaging might be what actually brings it down.

David: Well, there’s currently too little capacity to do that encapsulation. So you’ve got a backlog. These are supply chain constraints. These are very logistics-oriented things. So they’re raising money to deliver on time, hopefully on budget, $10.3 trillion worth of data centers, and they’re already dealing with some pretty significant issues. I mean, we’re talking about 2,933 projects either operational or planned. It’s a lot of projects.

Kevin: You remember Gary Larson, there’s a cartoon of a little kid climbing up onto the top of a slide. At the bottom of the slide, remember the spiders have made this big web, and the one spider says to the other one, “If this works, we will feast for weeks.” And in a way, what we’re talking about is this is a big project. Okay, you got the nets all settled, and if it works, we’ll feast for weeks. If it doesn’t work, it’s going to be a problem. Yeah.

David: It’s going to be a problem. So the scale of the build-out to support the financing commitments and the ramp-up in revenues from the data centers to support a growing quantity of debt, all that’s on a clock.

Kevin: Right.

David: And so we’ve said this in previous shows, where it’s one thing to invest heavily in CapEx spending out of your own war chest, but the dynamic shifts when you have to match up revenue inflows with revenue outflows. So when you hit the debt markets, that’s when the clock begins.

Kevin: Right. You’ve got your monthly payment. I mean, everybody who’s ever had a credit card understands that.

David: Yeah. Payments have to be made now and in the future, obviously on an increased scale as they’re adding capacity and adding to the number of projects brought to market.

So the author of this paper, he notes that as hyperscaler capital expenditures outgrow internal cash flow, financing is shifted towards leases, joint ventures, project debt, private credit, securitization, and special purpose vehicles. These structures expand funding capacity—so, I mean, that’s a positive point to make—but also raise asset-level leverage, obscure contingent obligations, and expose investors to tenant concentration, technological obsolescence—we’ll get more to that in a moment—execution delays—which is a lot of what I’ve just been talking about—and uncertain residual values.

Kevin: Okay. But you said he actually is economically analyzing this, saying, all right, for an investor in AI to get say 5%, let’s say 10% return, he gives the numbers of what would be needed.

David: For investors to get a 10% annual return, these projects have to generate 38.74% on the capital base. So, he’s assuming a 50% operating cash flow margin and mature annual revenue in 2032. That needs to land at $3.72 trillion.

Kevin: Which is a lot of m— I’m going to need to read this paper, I can tell. I’m going to have to sit and think about this stuff a little bit.

David: For sure. And please, read the paper. But the important thing to note there is that in terms of 2032 GDP, that’s 9.2% of GDP.

Kevin: Wow. And we were comparing that to those other projects.

David: If these projects are going to generate a 10% return annually for investors, they’re going to have to throw off $3.7 trillion, which is the equivalent of 9% of 2032 GDP.

Kevin: And the railroads took 2% of GDP, roughly.

David: So, we’re talking about an investor’s return and what that number would have to be as a percentage of GDP.

Kevin: To get that return, yeah.

David: If you’re talking about the annual spend, that is the 3.63%.

Kevin: Oh, I see. Okay. So, you’re talking about what would be—

David: So in the end, what you’ll spend to build it out.

Kevin: Okay. So almost 10% of GDP would be what the AI take would be if they’re making 10%.

David: Yeah. If we’re going to generate revenue, and this is going to work out for investors, and they’re going to make 10% a year, how much revenue do these have to throw off?

Kevin: Right.

David: It’s a lot of cake. That’s a lot of cake.

Kevin: Yeah. I wonder if these are at all reasonable numbers.

David: The author makes the case that these revenue requirements, they’re plausible, assuming that current pricing for frontier computation stays the same, which is a big ask. If you’re increasing the quantity or the supply of compute, how do you maintain the same— And we’re already seeing it with competition between Anthropic and OpenAI.

Kevin: Right. We’re calling for regulation right now.

David: With their newest models, they’ve cut their pricing by 40 or 50%. So, this paper may be dated in that sense because he’s assuming that the economics work as long as you can maintain your pricing power for daily GPU use. If you can’t—

Kevin: If you have to compete with somebody else, now you’re cutting into the numbers.

David: If you have to compete with the Chinese.

Kevin: Yeah, true.

David: Bit of an issue. So he makes the case that it works if, and there’s a big if. So, he says that the central economic question is instead whether demand is deep enough to absorb roughly 180 gigawatts of new capacity at high utilization. And whether providers retain sufficient pricing power for GPU, our prices to remain near current levels as capacity expands and competition amongst hyperscalers, cloud providers, and AI model developers intensifies. For context, given current estimates of combined revenues at OpenAI and Anthropic of around $100 billion, revenue would need to grow—these are his numbers—revenue would need to grow 80% per year until 2032. So that’s 80%, and then 80% on top of that 80%. This isn’t a compounded rate.

Kevin: Wow. 80, 80, 80 on the big number. Yeah, on the new big number.

David: To reach— Again, if we’re going to satisfy investors, get them their 10% rate of return, given the amount of capital that’s being committed, we’re going to have to see revenue amongst OpenAI and Anthropic grow 80% per year until 2032 in order to reach $3.725 trillion in revenue. And then he adds, “If the economic life…” This is really interesting. “If the economic life of IT equipment is shorter, the revenue requirement rises substantially.”

Kevin: So let’s put that in perspective, then, because these other projects that you’re talking about, a canal system, that thing lasts forever. A railroad, I don’t know how long— You have to have replacements. I mean, we have a little narrow gauge railroad here.

David: They’re fixing stuff, but it’s also been there for 120 years.

Kevin: It’s been there 120 years. So, a chip is almost out of date by the time it is packaged or it gets there.

David: It’s delivered, yeah. I mean, the last point, this is a true differentiator for this infrastructure build out. Canals, highways, railroads, once they’re built, they have 40-year lives—or more. A lot more.

Kevin: Right.

David: Data centers are broken down into two chunks. You’ve got the structures and you’ve got the guts inside. The structures include the buildings, the power infrastructure, the cooling systems, and you could generously assign a 20-year life. Maybe, it’s a little bit more than that.

Kevin: Here’s your building. Here’s your air conditioner. You got 20 years.

David: That accounts for 32% of the project costs. Sixty-eight percent of the project costs are IT equipment, which, using current accounting conventions, they estimate will last six years. Now, anybody who’s involved in technology hardware knows that if you’re still sitting on something that’s six years old, you’re a dinosaur. My kids make fun of me because my iPhone-

Kevin: Here’s my new iPhone, yeah.

David: My iPhone is six years old, and they look at me like I’m from the Stone Age. They’re surprised it even has a camera.

Kevin: And we’re talking about something where we’re—not just our companies competing here in the United States, but we’re talking about competing against other countries.

David: Yep. More conservative estimates are three to four years until obsolescence. So NVIDIA chips from three to four years ago, they’re already out of date. Nobody’s using those anymore. So your recurrent reinvestment, recurrent reinvestment in data center infrastructure is massive. You’re talking about 32% which is stable. Sixty-eight percent which you’re going to have to tap.

Kevin: Keep replacing every few years.

David: How much more money is involved just to keep it going? So this is on a scale we’ve never seen before, but of a very different nature because the structure and the guts are two different things. So, shift the economic life of the IT infrastructure from six years to three years, again, in terms of that refresh cycle. And your required revenue to deliver a 10% return to investors jumps to $6 trillion a year, which is, looking at 2032 GDP, 14.8% of GDP just to get your AI investors paid. That’s six trillion a year. Again, this is crazy.

Kevin: Okay. So what’s different right now, Dave? A canal system doesn’t solve its own problems, a railroad doesn’t solve its own problems. You had mentioned that you asked AI itself how to solve this problem.

David: Absolutely, yeah.

Kevin: So what did ChatGPT have to say?

David: All right. So full disclosure, I asked OpenAI, I asked ChatGPT how best to understand the 566 gigawatts of power generation. Actually, subtract that out for the delayed or canceled project, so the question I asked was only a total of 301 jigawatts.

Kevin: So, you were asking how—

David: [Wispered:] Jigawatts.

Kevin: You were asking how to open the pod bay door, right?

David: Yeah.

Kevin: Go ahead.

David: I mean, this is a disclosure because I have no way of verifying these numbers. This could be pure hallucination.

Kevin: But here’s what it has to say.

David: Here’s what it has to say. Assuming continuous annual power generation at 100%, which is totally unrealistic, your nuclear plants get maybe 90%. And then if you’re looking at solar or wind, maybe 25, 30%, because the sun doesn’t always shine and the wind doesn’t always blow. So that intermittency affects the effectiveness, the continuous generation, pretty dramatically.

But we’re going to assume continuous annual power generation at 100%. You would need 301 new nuclear power plants.

Kevin: Wow. And this is ChatGPT is telling you, “This is how we’re going to get it done.”

David: That’s to generate the power to drive the data centers which are scheduled to be delivered between now and 2032.

Kevin: Yeah. You would need 301 new nuclear power plants.

David: So, I’m just—

I don’t get this. The enthusiasm levels around AI— Okay. NVIDIA is selling lots of chips, right, but they’re not even being delivered to the data centers because they can’t get them encapsulated. So, where are they? But people keep on buying them like hotcakes, the prices are going higher. We’ve got the supply and demand dynamic. And the theme, the narrative of AI is so all-encompassing that people don’t think, “What does it take to generate the energy to run between two and three thousand data centers?”

Kevin: In this case, 301 new nuclear power plants, probably fewer Hoover Dams.

David: Only 143 Hoover Dams.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: 143 Hoover Dams.

Kevin: I’m sure we’ve got the water for that.

David: 602 gas-fired power plants or—

Kevin: I’m sure we’ve got the coal for that.

David: Friendly ChatGPT helps with this. 30,100 wind turbines or 602 million solar panels. And then I asked, “How much acreage does it take to put up 602 million solar panels?” It was kind of a qualifying question. I love these dialogues. My best friend is Chat these days. Well, if you put them right next to each other and don’t allow for any roads to service them or anything else, it takes a lot less. But conservatively, five acres per megawatt. So, that’s only 1.51 million acres.

Kevin: Which is, put it in perspective.

David: A lot of land.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: A lot of land.

Kevin: Wow.

David: Turbines cover 22.6 million acres, and that’s the entire state of Indiana.

Kevin: Okay. So turbines would take, it looks-

David: 30,000 turbines.

Kevin: Wow.

David: It would take 22.6 million acres.

Kevin: So, we could throw that Hoosier State out.

David: Listener right now has a friend who’s super interested in AI and thinks this is great. Right. Where’s the power coming from? And to achieve, I mean, we’re not even talking about artificial general intelligence. Just to get on board with what is slotted between now and 2032, where’s the power coming from? What does it take to get permitted to deliver that power? So hopefully, between the state of Indiana and the Hoover Dam, 143 of them, you’ve got a visual image for like, “This really is a big project.”

Kevin: Yeah, but if you’re two spiders at the bottom of the slide—

David: If this works.

Kevin: If we can pull his off—

David: We’re going to eat for weeks. Well, I think that’s what Sam Altman’s saying. If we can pull this off, we can eat for weeks? So, did I mention execution risk?

Kevin: I think that’s what we’re talking about. The spiderweb at the bottom of the slide.

David: And interest on the debt that is accruing even though revenue is not flowing yet to offset it. So the scale of the ambitions, they don’t match the physical. They don’t match the logistical constraints, let alone the costs.

Kevin: Right.

David: So I think last week illustrates this well. Oracle declares force majeure on a New Mexico project that it’s doing with Blue Owl.

Kevin: Okay. And so force majeure, you explained this earlier to us in the meeting. Force majeure is—

David: It’s an act of God that gives you an out in a contract obligation.

Kevin: You don’t have to pay because lightning struck.

David: Yeah. Nuclear war. Well, you can’t expect me to perform my obligations under the contract post nuclear war. Fair point. So, you’re no longer obligated under the contract to do what you’re supposed to do because of force majeure.

Kevin: But where was the act of God on this force majeure for Blue Owl? How do you do that?

David: Blue Owl may not be able to bring that project online within the scheduled time frame. The lease contract goes into effect even though the facility will not be operational. In July, Blue Owl was not given a natural gas pipeline extension by the state of New Mexico, which would feed the energy needs of the site.

Kevin: And that goes to “where’s the power?”

David: Yeah, this is a $165 billion project, 2.6, 2.5-gigawatt data center campus on 1,400 acres, and it’s scheduled to be online in 2028. So Oracle is declaring force majeure 18 months beforehand, which I think is very interesting. And by the way, they’ve put some things out on Twitter. They’re still publicly claiming the project remains on schedule, which begs the question again, why are they declaring force majeure—

Kevin: Right. Eighteen months in advance?

David: I think they want to keep a placeholder for the space without paying higher costs in the lead-up to the opening. So, kind of an escalated cost as you get ready to launch. I’m not sure that a future-tense failure to launch is sufficient to weasel out of payment obligations. And a lot of these obligations are what they would call “come hell or high water,” with hell-or-high-water clauses where it’s like, “It doesn’t matter what happens. If the end of the world happens, you still owe us the money.”

Blue Owl stepped out, raised the money. Blue Owl has bonds that require cash flow to be serviced, and the escalated payments from Oracle were built into the bond structure, the security of the lease agreement being sufficient to raise capital for the project. So lo and behold, Blue Owl bonds are trading at 90 cents on the dollar.

Kevin: Right. This reminds me of some of the things that happened in China with the real estate debt, doesn’t it?

David: Yeah.

Kevin: That same type of thing where all of a sudden they were paying hundreds of percent in interest per year just before they fail.

David: Right, right, where bond yields went higher and higher. Oracle bonds are only yielding about 8%. Credit default swaps for Oracle have gone from low-double digits to triple digits. They are on the move, but we should watch this because if it gets worse, Oracle bonds are already on the edge of getting kicked out of the investment grade category, which would migrate $120 billion in bonds from investment grade to the junk category. If that happens, on a downgrade to Oracle debt to junk status, you’re talking about many institutions which hold that paper today as investment grade, they’ll be forced to sell it.

Kevin: To whom? And this is where it goes to the bag holder that you’ve been bringing up.

David: And at what price?

Kevin: Yeah, and at what price.

David: Yeah. So forced liquidation of Oracle debt in the event of a downgrade, got to find a buyer because the institutions that have clauses which say you can only own investment grade debt, when you get the downgrade to junk, it’s to force liquidation. Once you’ve read the paper, you’ll be disappointed by how much detail and how many of the topics have neglected. It’s a great paper.

Kevin: Yeah, it sounds like a great paper. I can tell just talking to you, though, I’m going to have to read it. I’m going to have to sit and cogitate on each one of these things because we’re not talking just about debt. We’re talking about power needs. I was just talking to a client of mine who loves to study systems, and he says it really is just about inputs and outputs. And you analyze the inputs, you look at the outputs. This is systems analysis also. Are we going to get enough output out of this AI promise? I mean, you were talking about the AI dream is probably a nightmare based on the debt, based on the power needs. Are we going to get enough output is what I’m asking.

David: It’s a big project. We’re committing in the debt markets to build a $10 trillion infrastructure. It’s not clear that we can get the parts and pieces to deliver it on time, but we’re going to be paying interest along the way. It feels like if you needed perfect conditions to land this plane, you’ve got wind socks at opposite ends of the runway pointing the opposite directions.

Kevin: That happened to me once in Telluride.

David: That’s not a great place to have imperfect conditions. But to land this plane, you need perfect conditions. And what this paper says is, “Yeah, it’s possible.” And then he just asks a series of questions and you go, “Oh my gosh, this is massive.”

Kevin: The beauty, though, is he’s putting this to numbers. Okay, this is a guy, he’s from Columbia University. He’s a sharp guy and he’s putting this to numbers. And it sounds to me like even though he’s saying, yes, this could happen, this is a warning paper, isn’t it?

David: For sure. I read the paper and then I was going through some of my other reading and I came across two references, one a Wall Street Journal article and another, a Financial Times article, which both mentioned the paper. And I would’ve seen those and been like, I got to find that paper, but I already had it.

Kevin: And we’re going to put that in the links on the show.

David: September 25th from the Financial Times, there was another article titled “Okay, So Where Are All the Data Centers?” And it opens with this comment: “A theme we’ve touched on a few times is the mismatch between consensus forecasts for chip sales and US data center completion. Morgan Stanley measured the gap earlier this week by estimating the shortfall in available power, concluding that more than half of the GPU servers sold between 2026 and 2028 might not have anywhere to be plugged in.” Kevin, did we mention execution risk?

Kevin: Where are all the data centers? It reminds me of, remember Potemkin Village?

David: Yeah.

Kevin: Okay. That was Catherine the Great, wasn’t it, that they were trying to show that they had all these buildups?

David: Where are all the people?

Kevin: Yeah. Potemkin Village, but this Jefferies, this guy—

David: Morgan Stanley was one group that did some analysis that the article references. Jefferies is another analyst group. Their analysts took more of a 30,000-foot view. Actually more than that.

Kevin: So if you did that, if you had satellites back for Potemkin Village, you would see that they were just facades.

David: Yeah.

Kevin: Where are the data centers?

David: So that’s what they did. They took satellite imagery and they’re tracking data center construction sites, and they show 16 to 18 gigawatts of gross capacity being energized this year.

Kevin: We need what? 300 and something gigawatts?

David: 300 gigawatts. We’re going to have to pick up the pace. Extrapolating from land clearing for projects. Again, Jefferies sees the gigawatt in the low 20s coming online next year. Again, that’s not a pace that matches the spending.

Kevin: It’s not going to get you to the 300 gigawatts.

David: Again, it doesn’t matter if you’re using company capital. It doesn’t matter if Amazon wants to fund it and wants to burn money, but if you’re going to borrow money, you create this cash outflow to make interest payments. And if you’re not delivering product on time, where are the data centers? Kind of an interesting question.

So again, if they’re delivering in the low 20s next year, this is not at the pace that our Columbia professor assumes is necessary to hit the hyperscaler ambitions. There are too many friction points. So the Financial Times article highlights— It’s an almost comical point, which is that it’s chip packaging, which I mentioned a minute ago. The massive bottleneck is that chips once fabricated have to be shipped off and encapsulated, then shipped back. Did we mention last week that shipping costs are going up?

Kevin: Yeah. We talked about a million dollars a boatload basically.

David: Well, don’t you know that’s already dated?

Kevin: Yeah.

David: It’s a million two.

Kevin: Is it really? Wow.

David: Yeah. So if you’re doing that journey from the Middle East to Asia, it was 800,000 and then it was a million, now it’s a million two. I mean, we’re up 50% in terms of shipping costs in two weeks, but peace is on the horizon just after the midterms.

Kevin: Wow. Okay. But let’s go back to chip packaging because that’s just like you said, that’s almost humorous. It’s like, oh yeah, we just can’t package them.

David: There’s not enough capacity for this sort of interim step.

Kevin: Munch all you want. We’ll make more, but the problem is you still have to put it in a package like burritos.

David: Where’s the bag? We don’t have any bags. Stop by and pick them up yourself.

Kevin: That’s what you’re saying. Yeah, chips.

David: So you’ve got this critical supply chain bottleneck and the Jefferies analyst, his comment was, “The packaging bottleneck also helps explain the disconnect between semiconductor sales forecasts and data center execution.” So keep this in mind, next time you’re getting all hot and bothered about your investment in Nvidia or some other chip maker.

Kevin: FOMO.

David: They’re making a lot. Where are they going? Oh, we haven’t used them yet. You’re still making a lot. Well, yeah, sales projections are amazing.

Kevin: We just can’t package them and we don’t have the power.

David: So they’re not being delivered. They’re not being used. But we’re making a lot.

Kevin: But this is a dream.

David: I mean, can you imagine a Doritos factory?

Kevin: This is the dream, the AI dream.

The Doritos factory, they start financing retail purchases of chips, and you just see this mountain the size of Everest of—

Kevin: Chips.

David: I like their salsa verde. It’s unbelievable.

Kevin: Oh, you munch all you want then.

David: Oh man. I got in trouble with salsa verde.

Nevermind.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: Okay. “So the semiconductor analysts may see very large 2028 demand numbers”—this is coming back to the Jefferies analyst comment. “Semiconductor analysts may see very large 2028 demand numbers because hyperscaler orders, accelerator roadmaps and AI demand remain strong, but”—keyword—”but data center analysts must translate those chips into package systems, installed racks, electrical infrastructure, cooling interconnection, and energized land. Each conversion step reduces the near-term executable capacity relative to the headline demand.” This is— Right? The article concludes this way. “In the longer term, power availability is still the bottleneck, along with labor and transformers and cooling equipment.”

Kevin: And shipping costs.

David: And backup generation. “The gap between planned capacity and physical execution remains the central issue.”

Kevin: Okay. We do face something, though, Dave, that we’ve not faced before. A railroad was just a new form of transportation. A canal was just a way of delivering water. These were big costs. We’re now facing something that actually does tell you what to do next to solve the problem. And I’m wondering, I’ve been thinking about this, how is AI, the AI solutions to this, how’s that going to affect the way debt is handled?

So like these hyperscalers, they’re not just investing in AI, they’re probably using AI to find creative ways of getting this debt to work and getting these centers to work. Do you think that there’s going to be a change in the way the financial markets work based on the fact that you’ve got machines making all the decisions?

David: We had somebody from the ECB this week basically say, “We need to get ahead of this. We see the increased likelihood of financial market collapse if bots are doing all of our trading and we don’t have any kill switches.” So to your question and that point, I think there is a concern that probably goes back to the conversation we had with Jim Rickards where he’s looking at strategic threats, nuclear war, market threats, trading algorithms gone wild.

Kevin: Decisions that a human wouldn’t necessarily make, but a machine would.

David: And how do you shut it down? Do we have adequate kill switches to say, “All right, market’s closed.” Well, what if there’s a workaround to you shutting down the market?

Kevin: Right. But let’s go to the hyperscalers because that’s where the money is right now.

David: Yeah. I think the bigger issue with AI and the debt markets is they’re just gobbling up all of the available demand. If you’re talking about investors who have money to invest, there is demand for IOUs and they’re soaking it up.

Kevin: Well, we’ve talked about it’s even competing with the US Treasury markets. The government themselves are competing for that money to borrow.

David: Warsh mentioned it as much in his comments at the last meeting. So the last article making kind of a trifecta of reading on AI was also from the Financial Times. I think it’s from the 27th—it’s either the 27th or 28th—titled “AI Hyperscalers Are Transforming Debt.” It’s a great read.

There’s a couple of things that it does well. It underscores the interlinkages of AI debt throughout the global bond market. So this is not just a domestic US issue. We’ve got US hyperscalers. No, no, no. They’re tapping the debt markets globally.

Kevin: So they’re borrowing in other currencies as well?

David: Yeah. As hyperscalers issue huge tranches of debt in a variety of currencies.

Kevin: That’s a carry trade.

David: The key takeaway is the need to raise capital at such a scale that the hyperscalers are crowding out demand for other corporate debt offerings and sovereign debt. And because the hyperscalers are willing to pay more to get the cash fast because they are on a competitive time frame, it’s driving up interest costs globally. Now, that is not to say that they’re single-handedly responsible for the rise in global yields. They are one factor.

Kevin: It’s in addition to why sovereign debt has to have a higher yield.

David: Yeah. And corporate debt as well. And the crowding out is happening with longer-dated paper because the hyperscalers would like to finance on as long terms as possible. I forget if it was Google or Meta. One of the European offerings was a billion dollar, 100-year bond. I mean, we’re talking long term debt.

Kevin: Wow.

David: I mean, answer this. Where is AI in 100 years? I don’t know, but let’s give them money to find out. There’s an absurdity here.

Kevin: Well, where are the humans in 100 years? You said there’s a 10% chance this is going to annihilate the human race. They said it.

David: Let’s put a billion dollars on 100 years, we’ll be fine. I don’t know. I mean, the way people are handling their finances, the way people are investing in this, it just suggests that the power of this narrative is crowding out reason.

Kevin: That’s a good way of putting it.

David: And that’s a problem. So in the public markets with corporate debt, because they want to finance things on a longer-term basis, it’s forcing other corporations to finance shorter-term, which increases corporate rollover risk. If you have to refinance every three to five to seven years—

Kevin: Especially in a rising interest rate environment.

David: Because you couldn’t compete for the new issues of 20-year paper or 30-year paper or 100-year paper. That’s creating more rollover risk for other corporations in other sectors, which just is what it is. The paper’s going into the public markets. We’re talking about AI debt. It’s going into the public markets, it’s going into private credit vehicles. It’s going to pension funds, it’s going into insurance funds. And they love it because it’s higher yielding than Treasuries.

So, if weakness emerges in the sector, we are talking about Canadian and Australian and Swiss and British and Japanese and US debt markets all being implicated. So, earlier when I was talking about the global financial crisis and the mortgage-backed securities, asset-backed securities market and how those financialized assets got into so many portfolios around the world, you’ve got an influx of capital into the US to invest in hyperscaler equity and anything related to AI in the equity markets.

Globally, there’s demand for debt, it’s paying more. If there’s a problem in the space, it’s now multi-currency, multi-country, and multi-asset class. So, to keep their balance sheets, this is the AI hyperscalers, to keep their balance sheets looking clean, much of the debt that’s being offered is in special purpose vehicles. So, it doesn’t show up on their balance sheet.

Kevin: Right. So, bag holding again.

David: Well, it allows for the hyperscaler leverage ratios to look better than they are, and it allows them to maintain better credit ratings than they should be afforded and thus get better access to capital at cheaper rates.

Kevin: So, this boils down to: this better work because everybody’s involved.

David: Yeah. I mean, Torsten Slok, he’s the chief economist at Apollo— I like him, anytime I see him writing something, there’s something to learn. He brings interesting insights. He was quoted in this article saying, “The credit story of hyperscalers rests on a single consensus assumption that operating cash flow triples $600 billion to $2 trillion. If that doesn’t happen, then the risk is that the AI trade weakens”—I think that’s a polite way of describing it—”with credit spreads widening, CapEx plans getting cut, and ultimately US GDP slowing.”

So, we go back to Bessent, and he says, “We’re going to get 3% growth…” Yeah, I mean, we can get 5% growth, we can get 8% growth, there’s no limit to our growth as long as we’re doing it through an infrastructure spend that doesn’t have any limits. If you’re willing to spend five or $10 trillion, that spending shows up as GDP growth.

Now, the question is, if it was debt finance spending, what do you have for it at the end of the deal? An infrastructure build with rails, to your point earlier, all the railroad companies go broke. What do you have? Rails. Tens of thousands of miles of railroad that somebody’s going to own, somebody’s going to use, and it is going to open up the west—

Kevin: Canal, same thing.

David: If you were the equity or debt investor, you got wiped out, but there is an asset still there. In this case, we’re talking about 68% of the asset value being worth zero within five to six years, Generously five to six years. And it has to be replaced. This is nutsville.

Kevin: Okay. And then you’ve got— Let’s go back to the competing. The government’s going to have to raise how much this year? They’re going to have to borrow money as well. So, not just the AI markets, but there is this fiscal competition or the competition with the fiscal side.

David: Yeah. The crowding out in the bond market by AI debt offerings, it’s complemented—that’s the corporate bond market being crowded out—it’s complemented by the crowding out of fiscal authorities in the developed world as well.

So, the UK needs to issue debt, they’re now competing. Japan needs to issue debt, they’re now competing. The US is going to issue close to $2 trillion in debt this year. Combined, if you look at the Institute for International Finance, our $2 trillion plus another $8 trillion gets you to $10 trillion in debt being brought to market in 2026. That’s a global aggregate, which brings the total mountain of debt, $365 trillion is the new number.

Kevin: Well, okay. So, let’s talk also though about currency risk, Dave, because when you’re talking about debt, we are in a— Morgan Lewis talks about this here with your team. We are in a devaluation period of the dollar. And so, these debts are also denominated in a devaluing currency. What’s your thought on— I mean, I wouldn’t want to do anything other than really short-term debt at all, would you?

David: Right. Short-term T-bills. And even there it’s like, yeah, and keep your eye on the exits, have sufficient allocations to physical metals to where if you do see depreciation risk become a reality, five, six, 10, 20% a year—

Kevin: But no more than two year debt.

David: Or less.

Kevin: Maybe out to five?

David: No.

Kevin: Okay.

David: One, maybe two, I’d prefer one or less, 12 months or less. Keep it in T-bills.

Kevin: And when you guys are doing your management with T-bills, when we talk about Treasury—

David: It’s got to be very cash equivalent. And by the time you get out to two, three, four years, you start to see your pricing and duration risk. And I don’t know that that’s risk that you want to take in this environment, where the governments of the world have one solution to one big giant problem.

Kevin: Debasement.

David: The $365 trillion problem, to which, very nonchalantly, they’re just throwing another $10 trillion at this year. Nobody’s trying to solve the problem because they haven’t identified the problem as a problem. We have to wonder at the sanity of private capital sprinting towards the infinite money tree of AI. And I think you also have to wonder at the prudence of lending money to governments over any meaningful period of time, two, three, five, 10 years, when they have no plan to pay it back at its original value. They borrow money from you—

Kevin: Right. Pay it back in devalued currency.

David: —pay it back with interest. But what about the devaluation piece? The debasement trade is not a quarter opportunity, as in the next three months, that’s the way Wall Street talks about the debasement trade. “Hey, debasement trade’s back, and oh, now it’s gone.” No, it’s probably an accelerating quarter-century reality that affects the global middle class in a way that I think you could describe as a reset.

Kevin: Right. This is a paradigm shift for all of our culture. I mean, it doesn’t matter how old you are, you have not experienced this yet.

David: To solve $365 trillion in debt, you’re talking about the impoverishment of the global middle class via devaluation. We’ve already had the trade of the last 25 years, it’s been gold. Gold has done incredibly well.

Kevin: Yeah, four times better than the Dow.

David: And that thematic, that structural rise in the price of gold, it’s consistent with fiscal irresponsibility. And I think it’s getting geared up for another phase, where you also see it perform well in the context of consequences, the excessive risk taking in the equity and bond markets.

Kevin: So, what’s your conviction? What’s your conviction right now as far as, okay, the dollar, AI, bonds that would factor in interest rates, what’s your conviction on those? And then I want to hear your conviction on gold.

David: Well, I think those are all factors that lead me to a conviction level of 10 on gold. If someone’s considering selling gold today, they haven’t read the paper, or if they’ve read it, they haven’t understood what it said. We have so many fundamentals that are supportive—structural supports to the gold market. We mentioned last week, 289 tons of central bank demand in the second quarter, one of the largest quarters in history.

Kevin: And the Chinese buying.

David: Yeah. Annual imports already at a 1,000 tons— I said that wrong. Year to date imports already at 1,000 tons, which is more than annual imports.

Kevin: Wow.

David: Last year, the year before— They’re ramping up.

Kevin: They know something. Yeah.

David: What do they know? I think you have to buckle up. You have to assume that there’s some volatility in the price. System managers would rather you remain as a part of a captive audience, and discouraging moving out—

I mean, this week is an example. Shanghai Gold Exchange is closed from the 1st to the 7th. Could you see more volatility in the gold price as one of the primary gold buyers goes on vacation for a week? Yeah. Okay. Does that mean anything in the grand scheme of things? No, it doesn’t. It means that you could have a return to 4,000 or 3,900, or we could find ourselves tomorrow morning at 4,500.

I mean, whatever the volatility is, it’s meaningless. Because what is at stake both in terms of the US and global debt markets and this manic behavior as it relates to AI? This isn’t like a truism of all bubbles burst. If you look at the math of this paper, I don’t know how you don’t feel a little Chicken Little-ish. And it’s like, what? Who is actually—

Kevin: It’s almost wrong to call it a bubble, comparing it to past bubbles because this is so much bigger, Dave, and it’s global. Like you said, it’s global.

David: Don’t let short-term volatility shake you out. If you have a good gold position, keep it. If you don’t have a good gold position, add to it. Be as opportunistic as you can. Today’s a great day, tomorrow’s a great day.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: 400 points in either direction. I’m a happy buyer. Where we are next year— JP Morgan’s most recent price projections for the end of year, 6,000.

Kevin: And that’s JP Morgan.

David: Oh, but what about this week? Who cares? Who cares? So, I think conviction level 10, be mindful of the system managers wanting to keep you as a captive audience within a system that requires you as grist for the mill. I prefer the opt-out, I’m happy with ounces.

*     *     *

You’ve been listening to the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. I’m Kevin Orrick along with David McAlvany. You can find us at McAlvany.com and you can call us at 800-525-9556.

*     *     *

This has been the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. The views expressed should not be considered to be a solicitation or a recommendation for your investment portfolio. You should consult a professional financial advisor to assess your suitability for risk and investment. Join us again next week for a new edition of the McAlvany Weekly Commentary.

title.rendered: China Has Been Buying a Lot More Gold Than They Say

content.rendered:
Podcast: Play in new window

New research suggests China may hold far more gold than its official figures show, while its U.S. Treasury holdings continue to fall. This week, we discuss rising fuel costs and bond yields, the Fed’s latest rate hike, and why stock investors seem largely unfazed. We also look at troop movements in Europe, warnings from Poland, and the risk of a confrontation between Russia and NATO. A wider conflict could send gold lower at first, then bring investors back to it as financial pressures build. All of it raises a larger question: how much longer can governments keep adding debt at today’s interest rates?

  • Troop Movements to the Baltics, Poland Prepares for War, Tomahawks to Norway: You Figure It Out
  • Last Month, the CIA Director Was in Moscow to Warn Putin Not to Attack NATO
  • Stock Speculators Gleeful at Warsh’s Pseudo-Hawk Talk

“The diagnosis is debt. The solution is inflation. That’s the prescription. So I firmly believe inflation is a choice, it’s a policy preference, and it’s the only means of navigating $40 trillion in debt. Bessent may believe that GDP growth is the path to managing debt, but that would still require spending cuts in complement to growth, which our legislators have proven incapable of doing, leaving inflation the best pragmatic course, not the ideal course, but the most likely course. Warsh is not going to kill inflation, he’s going to dance with it.” —David McAlvany

*     *     *

Kevin: Welcome to the McAlvany Weekly Commentary, I’m Kevin Orrick along with David McAlvany.

David, this week there’s so much to talk about, and we probably want to keep this program less than an hour, so why don’t we hit the high points? But I mean, the interest rate rise, all the political events, the rumors about strokes with Chinese presidents, I mean, what do we believe and what do we do right now?

David: Yeah. Well, it comes as no surprise that fuel costs being volatile; interest rate costs being volatile; political popularity, or the populist movement, also being volatile; these are observable facts both in Europe and the US, and I think it’s not coincidentally.

Kevin: Yeah. And I’m thinking political leaders right now, everybody’s wanting to throw them under the bus. I’m thinking France, Germany, even here, even with Trump right now, the popularity rating is just plummeting.

David: If you look at Trump, you look at Merz, you look at Macron, just to name three, Trump’s net approval rating is either a net negative 25% according to the YouGov polls, or if you look at Nate Silver’s estimates, then he bases that on an average of 10 polling sources, is a more generous negative 20.3. And again, that’s on a net basis, so you’ve got 58% disapprove, 38% approve, the net negative is that 20% number. Then you look at a mere 14% that approve of Macron. The disapproval count is absent, but Macron has dramatically less support than Trump’s approval ratings imply here in the US. And Merz has an approval problem; he’s had that for a long time. 21% approval as far back as May of last year, and there was a recent regional election, he got 4.9% of the vote, that’s what he retained in the regional election.

Under the 5% threshold means that his party doesn’t even get a seat at the table, so the implication is that his approval as chancellor has plummeted since even the low numbers last May.

Kevin: So with Trump, do you think it’s inflation right now? I mean, I was talking to a client yesterday who said, “My gosh, Kevin, I’m paying seven bucks a gallon for diesel right now.” Is it inflation?

David: Yeah, I think Trump fails miserably in polls on inflation. He also gets low marks on the economy and trade. Unsurprisingly, he does far better on immigration, relatively speaking. If you’re interested in looking at those statistics, go to natesilver.net. Trump still has his one populist measure where he has a better relative showing, and certainly immigration’s an issue both in Germany and France. And I think that’s one of the things that you see about the rise of stronger right-leaning parties in those countries.

Kevin: So those leaders, Macron, Merz, and some of the other European leaders, they’re probably under huge scrutiny right now with immigration because that’s just been a disaster.

David: Right. And the inflation issues in France and Germany, the economic stagnation in both countries, yes, the immigration concerns, these are all points of high criticism among populist voters in Europe.

Kevin: Okay. So interest rates. Last week we saw an increase in interest rates, but that’s not just here, I mean we’re seeing it over in Europe as well.

David: I think when you look at interest rates, you can say, “Okay, well, what is this really a story about?” It’s a story about inflation. So fuel costs are emblematic. Fuel costs emblematic, rising interest costs come as no surprise in the context of rising inflation. Last week we had the French treasury yield, the yield spread to German bunds, it exceeded 1%, which is the largest gap since the European debt markets were under considerable pressure following the great financial crisis, so 2010, 2011, you had sort of a debt death spiral in Europe.

Kevin: Remember Greece?

David: Yeah. Well, French debt is now priced with greater concern than Greek debt is today.

Kevin: Wow.

David: Then you throw in Italy. Italy has a far worse fiscal problem than the French do, and yet its 10-year yield is less than the French yield. So the sovereign debt markets are telling a very important story, but again, if you wanted to look through what it’s really about, the consumer’s not happy, and the consumer’s not happy about inflation.

Kevin: And you’ve been talking about interest rate spreads, which it’s very important to watch that because you can see the difference between, say, junk debt versus Treasury debt, or you can see the difference between countries, so that would be the interest rate spread. But you’ve been bringing out on the energy side—I talked about diesel being seven bucks a gallon—a different kind of spread. What is it? As they refine, it’s called cracking?

David: Yeah, exactly. So fuel costs are something we’ve discussed previously with refined products priced even higher. The crack spreads for jet fuel, 53 bucks, diesel at 111. So the previous peak was 91, last week when we were talking about it, 101, this week, 111. So diesel at 111, that is a part of the populist pressure. Average cost for diesel in the US, $6.50 a gallon, in Europe, 9.50 a gallon, 9.50 a gallon. In at least one country, 10.50 a gallon. So again, that cost pressure is enough to continue to define the inflation trends in the months ahead, and as we mentioned last week, you also have the shipping costs on top of the crack spreads, which are an issue.

Kevin: You said it was like a million bucks a day to ship something with one of the big boats.

David: Well, again, these things changed. Last week it was 800,000, a new all-time high, now it’s a million dollars a day for the first time ever. Taking what in recent years was a one and a quarter million line item, 1.25 million was what it cost if you were going to ship the 25-day transit from the Middle East to China. Now you’re talking about 25 million instead of 1.25 million. That’s a 20X move in that line item. Who pays for it?

Kevin: So the listener who’s going, “All right, they keep skipping back between inflation, fuel costs, and interest rates,” but actually they’re all combined, Dave. When you’re buying a bond, let’s say a Treasury bond for 10 years, or, God forbid, 30 these days, you’re going to have to get an interest rate that beats inflation, and the inflation that’s coming from just the cost of diesel and getting this stuff across the ocean, a million bucks a day for one of the big boats, that turns into higher interest rates, doesn’t it?

David: Ultimately it does, because the bond market has to price in the cost of the time lag. And so we do see a higher move in interest rates in the short and intermediate term, so a flattening of the curve. So coming back to interest rates, the global bond market selloff hit its interim worst last week, and this is on the heels of or following the triple rate increase. We had the ECB early in the week, we had the Fed on Wednesday, we had the Bank of Japan on Friday.

Since then, the global bond markets have calmed down at least a little. US 30-year remains elevated, 5.28. The 10 year has stabilized just below 5%, spent most of last week above 5%. The two year at 4.74%, that’s a bit more concerning. The yield curve, as I said, has flattened over the last 30 days with shortened intermediate rates rising the most.

Kevin: Can you imagine trying to buy a house right now, what are mortgage rates at?

David: Well, and that’s where consumers confront this the most. I mean, certainly credit card rates go higher as well, but consumers see the 30-year fixed rate mortgage over 7%, that’s an impediment to refinancing. Refinancing is down 65% year over year. Thursday, we’re going to have the building permit numbers out and the new home sales figures out. I have to imagine less qualified buyers, there’s a less number of qualified buyers that exist as the cost of borrowing comes up into the sevens, but we’ll see.

Kevin: Okay. So you’re Trump right now, all right? Just pretend for a moment for me. You’re Trump. You’ve got the midterm elections coming right now. What do you appeal to when you’ve got mortgage rates over 7%, diesel over seven bucks a gallon in a lot of places, how does he appeal for the next few weeks before we get there?

David: Well, we’ve heard him say in recent days, prices are coming down, down, down, and I don’t know what prices he’s looking at. So he’s declaring victory, and yet he doesn’t have any data to support it. I think he’s got to lean into the upper part of the K-shaped economy. Asset prices are hovering near all time highs, and that’s where his list of successes begins. Perhaps that’s where it ends. Trading oil futures with the intent to drive prices down, this is something that the White House has been directly involved with.

Like the president’s working group on financial markets, keeping prices up while pressing other prices down, it’s an imperative with political benefits. It just depends if you want stocks and bonds to be performing well, this is an area where he definitely wants a footprint, he’d like to see oil prices lower, and he’s given traders a mandate to bring them lower in advance of the midterm. Can he do that in light of geopolitical events?

You find that he can be active in the trading pits, but where he’s not going to show up—the Oman crude price was $35 above the traditional Brent price because oil coming out of Oman through a choke point, you’re going to pay more. So you can control Brent, you can control WTI for trading futures contracts, but the real-world delivered barrel is a lot higher today because of some of the costs that we were talking about earlier.

Kevin: So when you get your gas, just remember that that gas got there dodging bullets, right?, with these choke points right now. Okay, but last week the Federal Reserve voted 12-0 to raise rates a quarter of a point. And Morgan Lewis, with your team here at McAlvany Wealth Management, gave us a briefing, and he said there is an agreement between Trump and Bessent and Warsh. And that agreement is obviously to try to manage the dollar lower without creating some sort of panic. The rising of rates, or the raising of rates, what signal is that showing right now?

David: Yeah, so last week the Fed’s decision, unanimous, 12-0, in favor of the 25 basis point hike, and certainly a suggestion that they weren’t done. So there’s no forward guidance, but there was a little bit of forward guidance. And it was important for two reasons. Number one, Warsh made clear that he understands the connection between credit, financial conditions, and their impact on asset prices and economic stability. So maybe for the first time in a generation of central bankers, he’s making clear that he gets that.

He basically underscored a comment that he made last August, “Money matters,” he said. “It’s not fashionable these days, but my view is that money has something important to do with monetary policy. We should pay attention to money created by the central bank, and money that comes from the banking and financial systems.” That’s what he said back in August. In the presser last week, he said, “We removed a dose of accommodation so that financial and credit conditions would be more consistent with our ultimate objectives.” But whatever chilling effect a hawkish tone might have had last week, Kevin, it was—

Kevin: It was short-lived.

David: Very short. Volatility for a day.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: The volatility index, the VIX, moved to a seven-week high of 19. The NASDAQ-100 dropped 1.5%. High-yield CDS jumped from 308 to 317, only to be reversed by Friday, as if the midweek warning was indeed a nothing burger. So VIX this week is back to the mid 14s, high-yield CDS back to eight, nine month lows. The NASDAQ-100 along with the MAG 7, all time highs. They’ve taken out both the June and the May highs, respectively. It’s like the risk markets hit a 25 basis point speed bump going 110 miles an hour. Business as usual.

Kevin: Right. So the risk guys are listening to him and going, “All right, how hawkish is he, and how hawkish can he be?” Something that they didn’t mention last week was the labor markets. There was no concern about it affecting employment if he raises rates, or GDP. So if you’re sitting there and you’re owning stocks, AI stocks or what have you, you’re going, “Ah, he’s sending me a signal that they’re not actually worried about slowing employment down. They’re not worried about the GDP falling right now.” Like you said, business as usual.

Okay, but yesterday you did a television interview, and the commentator asked you about thoughts about a 30% to 50% decline on the stock market. What was your response—that was basically being thrown back at you because you had made comments in the past on that?

David: Well, I provided notes for them ahead of time saying this is a probability, 30% to 50% declines in equities. So they asked me the question, and I said, “No, not unless or until the AI narrative falters or liquidity meaningfully tightens.” If you look at the Chicago Fed’s Financial Conditions Index, it’s still registering levels last seen in the fourth quarter of 2021 in the everything bubble, the meme stock craze.

Kevin: Money matters.

David: This is the age of SPACs where your blank check companies raise a couple billion dollars and it was very much like what we had during the South Sea Bubble, raising money for a concern, the purposes of which have yet to be determined. There was language like that back then.

Kevin: And people getting rich with that, “what was the South Sea Bubble?” And nobody could explain it.

David: It doesn’t matter. It’s going to be great. With the blank check, the SPAC, you could raise money and say, “It’s going to be for anything and we’ll put it to good use.” And people are like, “Yes, get me in.”

So that’s Q4 2021. You’d have to go back to Q1 2014. Again, we get through the European debt crisis. Financial conditions are incredibly loose. You had the head of the ECB promise to do anything to solve the problem, and conditions were incredibly loose. That’s what we have today, very loose financial conditions and a 25 basis point move higher doesn’t touch it. So for clues to tightening, we’re going to have to continue to watch the bond market.

Kevin: Well, it was interesting when you interviewed your guest Gamble, you remember that a few weeks ago? He said that right now the Treasury market is competing for the money that’s going into the AI side of things. Right now, between the Japanese having to sell off Treasuries to intervene on the yen, money matters. Warsh was right, money does matter, and money right now is going into that AI side of things and not into Treasuries. There’s pressure there, isn’t there?

David: That made its way into the Fed’s comments last week as well. In the presser, he starts talking about geopolitical issues driving prices higher in the bond market. He does talk about there being a competition and AI squeezing into the space, competing with Treasuries, yields going higher. I thought it was very interesting that he didn’t say anything about there being fiscal issues as a part of the pressure.

Kevin: Like spending more on our interest on debt than our entire military. He didn’t mention that.

David: Or having 1.8 to $2 trillion in deficit spending in a period of time where we’re not in a conflict like World War I, World War II. If you look at what we’re adding to our deficit spending, the only time we’ve done that is in the context of the pandemic or World War I, World War II.

So we are spending at those levels. That is a fiscal problem, and there was silence. Maybe he was really implicitly saying, “I’m going to stay in my lane. There’s no reason to critique them,” but it is a significant factor in the upward pressure in interest rates.

Kevin: Well, how about the comment with China on weaponizing the dollar? Is that possibly why people are backing away from it?

David: I think with pressure on interest rates, we’re talking about the supply side being too great. There’s also the demand side. So pressure on Treasuries. Reported by Bloomberg last week, foreign holdings of Treasuries dropped 50.4 billion on the latest reading. Probably not a surprise, France and Canada hitting the exits. China did too. 15.4 billion was reported, Chinese liquidations in July.

We’ve already discussed the Bank of Japan dumping Treasuries to support the yen. Add to that the New York Times quoted the IMF’s former head of the China division there at the IMF. He pointed towards geopolitical factors and US weaponization of the dollar through financial sanctions causing central banks and other official investors to diversify away from dollar assets. So you’ve got the demand side diminishing, the supply side continuing to increase. Of course, these are relevant factors driving interest rates higher. And that’s what we’ve been saying since 2022.

Kevin: And 2022, of course, is when Putin went into Ukraine and we did weaponize the dollar. So it cuts down on people wanting to buy. We have to raise rates to increase demand, basically, for US Treasuries. How stingy can the Fed talk? How hawkish can they actually be, and not tumble the markets?

David: And again, you say we have to raise rates. The Fed is embarrassed if they don’t. So they moved interest rates 25 basis points. Relative to the two year, they’re still 75 basis points behind schedule. The bond market has already done the lifting. The bond market has already said interest rates should be 100 basis points higher. That’s where reasonable compensation is for the inflation and duration risk that we’re taking. Now you need to catch up.

And that, in essence, is the hat tip that the Federal Reserve gave last week. But how the Fed gets more hawkish or stingy, even as the Treasury gets more needy, that’s going to be interesting to see play out. We suspect—you mentioned it earlier, Morgan’s comments—we suspect that they’re discussing the appropriate choreography, how they work together in this delicate dance.

Kevin: Well, and Morgan, he calls it fiscal dominance. And fiscal dominance is just simply that the Fed’s going to have to tend to the fiscal side of things before they do the inflation side. So maybe the hawkish stuff is talk. It’s more talk than action.

David: I would say that if you’re not reading Hard Asset Insights on a weekly basis, that should become a part of your Saturday routine. In this week’s Hard Asset Insights, the mixed message from the Fed was number one, there is this timelier return to the inflation target via interest rate increases. So that’s why they’re raising rates, helping with a timelier return to the inflation target.

At the same time, they’re pushing out the timeline on reaching the inflation target, which is embedded in the summary of economic projections. And they moved that from 2028 when they thought we were going to get to the 2% target. Now it’s 2029.

That might actually offer an explanation for why risk assets, stock market in particular, are not concerned about the rate hike because you can actually see in the details, in the fine print, the Fed’s not really serious about this. Tapping on the brakes is different than slamming on the brakes, and that’s what we had last week was tapping on the brakes. The Fed has expressed that a rate hiking cycle is not going to impact economic growth, which, again, suggests that this is not a Volcker-esque cycle.

Kevin: Yeah, Volcker slammed on the brakes. Volcker was the Fed chairman when I first started working here. And as we’ve spoken before, the difference between the Volcker years and now is the country had a trillion in debt at the time that he spiked rates and slammed on the brakes. You can’t spike rates and slam on the brakes when you’ve got 40 trillion in debt. That’s a lot of interest that would have to be paid.

David: Well, and again, for the Warsh Fed to say that this hiking cycle is not going to impact economic growth, the whole purpose of a real hiking cycle—a real hiking cycle—is to do just that. You slow the economy by raising the cost of capital in order to ease the inflationary pressures.

Kevin: But the dirty secret, Dave, is that inflation is a policy decision. I was just explaining that about an hour ago to one of the people who work here. It’s like, no, no, no, the question came, when do they plan on solving this? And it’s like, solve it? Why would they solve it? They can spend more money than they actually take in in taxes, but they have to use financial repression.

David: The diagnosis is debt. The solution is inflation. That’s the prescription. So I firmly believe inflation is a choice. It’s a policy preference, and it’s the only means of navigating $40 trillion in debt.

Bessent may believe that GDP growth, 3% is his number, GDP growth is the path to managing debt, but that would still require spending cuts in complement to growth, which our legislators have proven incapable of doing, leaving inflation the best pragmatic course. Not the ideal course, but the most likely course.

Warsh is not going to kill inflation. He’s going to dance with it. Of course, that’s going to be to the Treasury Department’s benefit. And of course he’s got help. The BLS will redefine it. The asset markets may well continue to celebrate it. What is he really doing? He’s posturing. He’s pretending. Warsh will be sincere whether he means it or not.

Kevin: Okay. So I’m going to shift to a new word. At least, it was a new word for me. I mean, you’ve heard the word “irregular warfare” going back decades. And we both have a friend who was a general in the Air Force who was known for a form of special irregular warfare. But I’m hearing something now called hybrid warfare, and Macron especially is talking about it. But part of what made this last week so unsettling, to be honest with you, is we’re hearing saber-rattling that might turn into a Russian NATO-type of attack. This hybrid warfare, this claim, would that draw the NATO nations in against Putin possibly?

David: Well, so going back across the pond, it’s an odd list of concerning events from last week and into this week. Le Monde reports that Emmanuel Macron’s growing concern is with a Russian hybrid attack against France. And Macron on Friday, and that’s the 18th, he convened a confidential briefing to discuss the matter. Closed door, don’t know what he said, but it’s a concern. Politico reports that NATO is “ready” for a Russian false flag attack. Meanwhile, the US has just deployed Tomahawks to Norway. NATO reconnaissance equipment is moving to both Germany and Latvia. You’ve got an inordinate number of German troops headed to the Baltics. You’ve got Polish and Finnish leaders warning that Russia is preparing for something. And you have to go back a little—

Kevin: Well, and we’ve got the CIA. We’ve got the CIA literally going over and talking to Putin. When has that happened last?

David: Yeah. So August 26th, this is a little dated, but the CIA director was in Moscow specifically to warn Putin not to attack NATO. So it’s August 26th. His last visit, if I’m not mistaken, was in February of 2022, just before Russia invaded Ukraine.

Kevin: So not very effective last time.

David: Well, what does the CIA know? They knew it was coming with Ukraine. Why is Europe mobilizing? Last week, we had the Polish prime minister give a speech stating that Poland was preparing for everything. And of course, they’ve already been at the receiving end of Russian hybrid warfare. European leaders are vigorously discussing Article V and trying to establish that hybrid warfare does not trigger the cooperation agreement among member states. They realize that this is something that is happening and is likely to happen more, and they don’t really want to get into a war with Russia.

Kevin: Well, okay. So this is interesting too though. Putin obviously knows there’s something up, too. You never know in these types of situations. We might be reading the news from our side of things, but he might be being drawn into something, too. I know that there’ll be plenty of comments who get angry about that, but when these types of things go on, you’ve got an awful lot of false flagging. And Putin came out and clearly said that that is not his intention. Now, of course, you can’t trust his word, but isn’t that interesting that he made a statement?

David: Well, save the best for last. Russian Embassy released this on Saturday from Vladimir Putin. He said, “Some leaders openly state that they are preparing for war with Russia. In my view, they’re simply trying to shore up their declining ratings by covering up failures in economic and social policy.”

Let me pause there. Yes, there is an issue with declining ratings, and yes, there is an issue with social policies and economic management. So yeah, he’s kind of hitting in where it already hurts, but he goes on to say, “Russia has no aggressive intentions towards European countries. We simply have no grounds for this. We are ready for cooperation and for restoring relations with our European neighbors.”

Kevin: I think somebody needs to write a book about history, and just publish the denial that occurs right before the very event that they’re denying. Right? You could write a book.

David: As I was reading that quote from Putin, I had another quote from Hard Asset Insights still echoing in the back of my mind. Morgan, the author of HAI, said, “Recall the old aphorism. ‘Never believe anything in politics until it has been officially denied.'”

Kevin: And that can be applied to more than just war. Remember when Nixon took us off the gold standard, and he said the dollar will be just as strong in the future as it— I know I’m misquoting, but he said it’s not going to affect the value of the dollar at all.

David: And he said this was a temporary move.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: Arguably, it is temporary. It’s just taken from 1971 to the present. We may be going back to the gold standard, or we may not. But—

Kevin: Okay. So I read a book—

David: Temporary is through the eye of the beholder.

Kevin: I read a book about a British special forces team that went in in the first Iraqi war. It was a fascinating book. I think it was called Bravo Two Zero. But the British, I didn’t realize this, when they fly them in behind enemy lines, these special forces teams, they stop and they take a 10-minute, what they call appreciation, and say, “Okay, what’s in the room? What’s on the horizon? What’s around me?” They just sit there. They don’t do anything except for taking appreciation. Now, I want you to do this right now for this last week. Europe, let’s take an appreciation. Let’s just say what’s going on around us, Dave?

David: So the appreciation is the part of what others have called the OODA Loop. I actually have this written on my window—

Kevin: Oh, that’s what you were looking at.

David: —just in my office.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: I come and go out of my office every day, and I look at the OODA Loop: observe, orient—that’s your appreciation—decide, act.

Kevin: That was actually written by a US fighter pilot. I can’t remember who it was, but I’m recognizing that.

David: So we’ve got troop movements to the Baltics, Tomahawks to Norway. Maybe the Greenland Security Agreement is a coincidence, but the CIA—

Kevin: Good timing.

David: —director in Moscow is not. Even if that’s a month dated, pressure is building. In the last 10 days, you’ve got Ukraine, which has taken at least 1.3 million barrels of refining capacity offline from its recent attacks. That’s just the recent ones.

Kevin: Yeah. And we’re having to tell Zelenskyy to stop it. It’s like, what a weird world.

David: Midterms are too close. Midterms are too close. Don’t defeat the enemy because it may mean that I get defeated in November. Our party gets defeated in November. Cool your jets.
