Kevin: How about the rumors about Xi possibly having a stroke when he was in India?

David: I mean, this may be stupid, but sounds like the rumors of Xi Jinping and his stroke in India during the BRICS Summit this weekend, maybe that’s overplayed. But if he fails to meet with Trump in two days, I think we can rethink that. I’m thinking about Putin again, because if Xi’s influence over Putin were to wane, I think you’re looking at Europe becoming a lot more volatile.

Kevin: Dave, we were talking last night. Okay. One of the beauties of being in gold and silver is there are some really interesting stories with coins. And there was a mystery coin of the 20th century that had just disappeared after the Nazi attack on Poland and Danzig, which is right there in the bay where Poland is. We had someone who found that stash of coins that Danzig had minted. It’s a fascinating story. I have some for the kids, just to tell the story, not to speculate on price.

But I went back. When we got that mystery coin that had disappeared for so long, I went back to look at, what is the history of Danzig? Why did they mint a coin, just a few thousand of these coins, to declare their independence? And it took me to September of 1939. And there had been an agreement, and I’m speaking about false flags here, and Putin and Russia, and just possibly a rhyming part of history as we talk.

The Germans had full intention to attack Poland, and they actually had full intentions to go on and attack Russia after that. But they promised not to do both at the Munich Summit a year earlier, back in August.

David: Oh, is it Munich or Berlin?

Kevin: No. I checked. It was Munich. Yeah. So, this is when Neville Chamberlain came out and said, “There will be peace for our time.” Well, they had promised, they had come up with an agreement, Neville Chamberlain. It’s the famous picture. He held it up and he said, “I’ve got the agreement. We’re good.” Well, the way the Germans justified attacking Poland after saying that they wouldn’t do it is SS officers dressed up in Polish uniforms and attacked a German radio station.

And then Hitler basically said, “We have no other choice but to defend German citizens.” It was a false flag. And it wasn’t confirmed as a false flag until the Nuremberg trials years later when the war was over. It was a Himmler plan. Himmler came up with it. But I’m just wondering at this point, are we going to see a false flag where Putin denies that he has any intention, it’s not in his best interest? Are we possibly going to see something happen where he says we have absolutely no choice but to defend ourselves, and bring NATO in?

David: I think about gold. Obviously, I think about gold a lot, but what is the next $500 move in gold? And as a thought experiment, if you start with a Russian false flag, like the one you’ve described in 1939, NATO members engage under Article 5. They’re trying to weasel out of that right now. What if the casualty count amongst civilians is such that NATO has no choice? So, NATO members engage under Article 5. Russia-Ukraine becomes a Pan-European conflict.

This gets interesting. Trump then retracts his threat to withdraw half of troops from Europe. Of course, that would be in exchange for extortion-level trade deals, but he could get whatever he wants. If you’re talking about taking an 80,000 troop count down to 30,000 or 40,000, well, we’ll leave them there. However, here’s the conditions that we stay. The euro buckles in the context of conflict. Obviously, the fiscal pressure that’s already there. We were talking about it earlier. The Italians are at 139%.

What do you think the French debt to GDP ratios are, the Italian debt to GDP ratios are on the other side of conflict? Give it six months, and they’re spending to save their lives. It’s an existential threat. People don’t think about what’s in the bank or not. You just print. You just print.

Kevin: Right. It’s an emergency.

David: The euro buckles, the dollar spikes. This gets interesting. Russians sell gold to fund a broader conflict. Gold could initially drop, then investors scramble back into the metals as global inflation—driven by not only the conflict, but energy shock 2.0, or maybe it’s 3.0 by that point—cripples the financial markets. We’re worried about a lack of demand for sovereign debt, and we’re worried about too much supply of sovereign debt right now. What about wartime deficits?

Kevin: Right. Who funds those? Yeah.

David: The thought experiment, maybe it’s a waste of time, but geopolitics is always unpredictable. Maybe in this case it’s more predictable. What I’m certain of is that, with or without expanded global conflicts, sovereign debt is already circling the drain.

Kevin: Right.

David: When there’s broad recognition of that, gold will have no ceiling. When there is a broad recognition of that, gold will have no ceiling. We’ve said for some time, central bank demand has, to this point, held the floor under the price. It’s investors that are going to define the ceiling.

Kevin: I’ve been thinking about this, too, Dave, because you and I talked last night about could gold actually drop if we had this conflict breakout? And you’re like, “Absolutely. Russia’s going to have to fund it somehow.” But I look at China, Dave, and China’s never told the truth about how much gold they’ve been buying—ever. I mean, we could watch it year after year and they’d say, “Oh, yeah. Official buying is this. It’s about this big.”

David: Or they don’t report it for three to five years and it looks like it’s zero.

Kevin: So, China, we’re talking about sovereign debt circling the drain, but China has been selling Treasuries and adding gold consistently month after month and they’re adding more and more.

David: Yeah. I think it was 2013 that they— Maybe it’s 2014.

Kevin: No. it’s 2013. Listen, I’ve got the scars. You’re talking about April?

David: No, no, no. They got to a peak of US Treasury holdings of about $1.3 trillion.

Kevin: Okay. I thought you were talking about the gold blast.

David: No. Now, they’re down to about 618 billion, off of 1.3 trillion. So, they have been selling Treasuries for some time. I read a research report this morning from a group called Metals Focus, and it was showing Chinese official demand over the past 10 years. Suggestion in this research piece was that it’s been understated by a significant margin. 2,306 tons was the official number in tonnage, year-end 2025. Add 80 tons to that because they’ve been aggressively buying this year. This paper says, “That’s probably closer to 3,862 tons.” That’s what the research piece suggests is the actual holdings, bumping their percentage of reserves in gold from 9%, which is what the world thinks it has, to over 19%.

They’ve arrived at that projection based on the imports over the last 10 years versus the end demand where they can count the ounces which have gone into investment, gone into jewelry consumption, and there’s an interesting difference in the numbers. Where did the rest of the gold go? If it didn’t go into investment demand, if it didn’t go into jewelry demand, where is it? Assumption being that the official reserves are understated.

Kevin: Yeah. Well, and I wonder, Dave, can we afford? You and I and any of our listeners, who cares if gold were to drop right after Russia, if there was an exchange, how could I possibly afford not to have gold reserves, just like China? China may understate the percentage of their reserves that they hold in gold. I think that’s probably a good policy for all of us, don’t you think? Understate to everyone around you what your actual reserves are, and keep adding.

David: Yeah. You can look at this through the lens of monetary regime change and the very deliberate move Chinese have had out of Treasuries and into gold. You can’t really separate out the financial, the fiscal aspects, the reserve management aspects, with what is the power structures around the globe shifting.

There is no doubt that the Chinese aspire to being not only a global player respected amongst peers, but the global player. So, what does this mean exactly? I think gold as a reserve asset is particularly important in uncertain times. The case for fiscal and geopolitical uncertainty is compelling, and I think so is the case for gold.

*     *     *

Kevin: I would agree. You’ve been listening to the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. I’m Kevin Orrick along with David McAlvany. You can find us at mcalvany.com, M-C-A-L-V-A-N-Y, .com and you can call us at 800-525-9556.

*     *     *

This has been the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. The views expressed should not be considered to be a solicitation or a recommendation for your investment portfolio. You should consult a professional financial advisor to assess your suitability for risk and investment. Join us again next week for a new edition of the McAlvany Weekly Commentary.

title.rendered: China’s 22 Month Gold Buying Streak

content.rendered:
Podcast: Play in new window

  • Trump To Warsh: Be A Patriot & Lower Rates
  • Bond Market To Warsh: Raise Rates Or Face The Consequences
  • Take Your $5,000 Trump Dividend & Buy An Ounce Of Gold

China is now on its 22nd straight month of gold buying, even as prices climb and central banks continue adding to their reserves. David McAlvany looks at the pressure building on Kevin Warsh and the Fed as Trump calls for lower rates while the bond market pushes the other way. Rising oil prices, inflation expectations, and a 10-year Treasury above 5% are making the Fed’s next move increasingly difficult. And with talk of a $5,000 Trump dividend, the question is whether that check would still buy an ounce of gold by the time it arrives.

*     *     *

“France, Italy, Poland, Spain, Germany, they all have elections this next year. And so I think the ECB wants to stay on top of radical political change resulting from inflation reactionism. They’re trying to get out in front of the inflation issue. I mentioned the 2.9 bumping to 3.3 across the eurozone. Bank of Japan is expected to hike rates later this week. Bank of Canada is on the horizon. Probably the only standout because they’ve got very weak labor markets—their economy is not doing well—would be the Bank of England. They may hold pat because their economy’s very much under pressure. The US would then stand out if it didn’t. I think the key for financial markets coming into this discussion with Warsh and the decision from the Fed, what we’ll find out in the commentary and in the Q&A is how he sort of cushions the decision.” —David McAlvany

*     *     *

Kevin: Welcome to the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. I’m Kevin Orrick along with David McAlvany.

David, we just walked out of the meeting. We get a briefing on Tuesdays. Morgan with McAlvany Wealth Management, you do the briefing. And I was thinking as I was listening to you guys talk that China reminds me of a master poker player right now, with the sunglasses on, not really betraying what they’re doing. And I want to talk about what they’re doing with some of the oil refining types of things, but let’s talk about gold.

David: Definitely. You look at what they’re doing in the oil markets, we’ll talk about this in a few minutes, and it’s been masterfully played. And I think they’re also in a unique position as yields rise with the yen to become very competitive in terms of carry trade and to borrow in Chinese currency at very low rates, now multiple percentage points below the US Treasury. There’s traction being gained.

Kevin: So for decades it was Japan, and now what we’re seeing is China’s moving their way in there. I mean, they’re on their 22nd month of buying gold, and price doesn’t seem to be affecting them.

David: No, and that’s a good point. So there’s some dynamics that are improving in terms of their capital markets, and you’re seeing more demand year over year, a huge bump up in demand for their dim sum and panda bonds. This is the products that they are able to sell outside of China. And so that is one thing. Another factor is internally they continue to be very acquisitive with the metals market 22 months in a row. I think we just mentioned it last week. The July numbers were 20 tons, and August came out just this week, and 650,000 ounces.

Kevin: And that’s the most since 2023, isn’t it? I mean for that, yeah.

David: Big purchase. And if you look at cumulative central bank purchases for the second quarter, three months ending June, you’re talking about one of the largest quarterly purchases, 289 if I’m not mistaken, 289 tons. It’s a lot. So the movement towards gold is there. Morgan made a great point, which was that a lot of their acquisitions were in an up market here in the month of August, and they’re not particularly price sensitive. They want the ounces.

Kevin: So any dips that we see in the gold market right now are buying opportunities because going forward, just the debt, the interest rates, the inflation.

David: Yeah, I would suggest that for individual investors that’s certainly the case, and you want the best price possible. I understand that.

Kevin: Okay. So Morgan said something that I think we should start with today because a lot of times, especially with the old Summers-Barsky paper that you’ve talked about, the idea would be if interest rates rise on US Treasuries, then gold should go down. But actually that’s if the US Treasury is still like gold, and it’s no longer being trusted like gold. There’s been a change in this environment of rising interest rates, possibly, where gold might rise with interest rates, not fall.

David: Right. And his distinction is between a healthy system and an unhealthy system. In a healthy system, Summers-Barsky holds, your real yield differential is compelling. You have to start looking at opportunity cost and saying, “Well, I’m sitting on ounces of gold here and yet I could make real income over here.” And so, at a certain threshold, it becomes compelling and money shifts, again, all things being equal, if we had a healthy fiscal backdrop. In the context of an incredibly unhealthy fiscal backdrop, it is different, and the possibilities of rising interest rates propelling gold higher, not being an impediment to it, is very much a possibility.

Kevin: So this week the ECB is probably going to raise rates or has.

David: They did raise rates 25 basis points.

Kevin: We are probably going to raise rates here coming up. So the short term moves in the gold market or the inflation statistics, what have you, we need to look longer term.

David: Yeah. I think last week the ECB set what was likely a precedent amongst central banks, raising rates 25 basis points to 2.5%. Inflation in the eurozone rose to 3.3% from 2.9. That was in July. And so, the market is now p ricing in a 75% probability of an additional increase by the ECB in October, 73% probability of an increase in December. This week, the Fed has to face the fact that looking through the oil shock from the Iran conflict might have been a mistake. And with the conflict not being as short lived as expected, with inflation psychology shifting amongst households who now expect a 4.6% inflation rate going forward, should that psychology become entrenched, inflation expectations become something of a self-fulfilling prophecy. So on trial this week is monetary policy independence. You get the president who has complicated the calculus with his comment: the Fed board with its great new leader must get smart.

Kevin: He wants them to be patriots. He wants them to lower those interest rates, by golly.

David: Be patriots for a change. High interest rates put the US at an unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen.

Kevin: Yeah. You know what it reminds me of? It reminds me of George Bush when everybody got 100 bucks and he’s like, “Be a patriot and go spend that 100 bucks.” It’s like, patriotism has really changed since I studied it when I was a kid. All right, so let’s go back to this never-ending war. In reality, things are spreading, not getting smaller right now.

David: Well, just one more note on patriotism. I went to the kids’ Civil Air Patrol meeting last night, and it’s just interesting to me. There are still these pockets within American culture. They opened with prayer, and then three minutes later there is the pledge of allegiance to the flag. And I thought, that used to happen every day in grade school for me. And my guess is that there’s such a shaming about being an American today or having some respect for what our past is, the differentiation in terms of the historical progression and evolution. “We don’t feel comfortable doing that. It wouldn’t be right. You’re going to infringe upon the sensibilities of this diverse culture of ours.”

Kevin: Well, and part of patriotism, somebody brought this up the other day, was volunteerism, and Civil Air Patrol, I was involved with Civil Air Patrol for years, as you know, flying with them. And you had guys who were really sacrificing a lot of time to help somebody who might be lost or have crashed out into the woods. So it’s good, but volunteerism, it’s the same type of thing where you’ve got people who are actually saying, “Look, I don’t need to get paid. I want to help somebody.”

David: Yep. No, it’s “be patriots for a change, lower interest rates.” That’s an interesting conception of patriotism.

Kevin: Yeah, that’s form of patriotism.
