What I find super interesting: the rest-of-world holdings. If you look at debt and equity, of the 191 trillion, rest-of-world holdings—so foreign capital in our markets—63.89 trillion, call it 64 trillion. Foreign holders of US assets account for 33% of the total.

Kevin: Look at the equity markets, though, look at AI. It’s the shiny thing, right?

David: Yeah. Well, we used to be considered the shining city on the hill. I’m wondering if we’re clearly not the shiny object on the hill.

Kevin: You know what about shiny objects though? Once it’s not shiny anymore—

David: People move on.

Kevin: And you said it’s 33% foreign holding?

David: Yeah. So, how constant are those capital commitments? That’s going to be critical to US financial market performance, both stocks and bonds. And I wonder if central banks aren’t the first movers out of US assets, where you’re looking at a lot of foreign capital still happy to chase the AI trade and happy to chase higher yielding mortgage-backed securities, agency paper, even corporate bonds.

The flows are still there, but I wonder if central banks are moving out of US assets first. There’s no doubt that as long as the AI narrative remains captivating, a huge part of that 64 trillion is going to be happy to harvest the higher returns.

Kevin: Do you think it is remaining captivating? I mean, it’s interesting how it’s having to be talked up at this point far more than originally. Even Trump, he’s trying to convince everybody that AI is a great thing. And why does it have to be talked up if the narrative is already there?

David: That was a great bit of commentary, too. Anybody who’s negative against AI, this is conspiracy-theory stuff. People who are most negative this week were the two CEOs of Anthropic and ChatGPT.

Kevin: The guys right in the middle of it.

David: Yeah. OpenAI and Anthropic are like, “Yeah, we do have some security concerns, and our Frankenstein’s getting off the leash.”

Kevin: Maybe they’re not patriotic. Could be.

David: It’s so interesting. But just as the AI CapEx spending has accounted for the majority of GDP growth in recent years, so too has the AI trade accounted for most equity index gains, certainly for this year.

Kevin: That’s called concentration, isn’t it?

David: For sure. And it’s skewed when capital comes in and it buys an index. Most of our indices are capitalization weighted, so the bigger the capitalization, the more capital flows they get with any new incoming funds, which was sizable. Second quarter, incoming capital from overseas, 4.49 trillion. That is a lot of money. Three and a quarter of that, 3.27 trillion went into equities. The remainder, debt and repo markets, they made up the rest.

Notably, 79 billion in Treasury liquidations for the quarter. This is not central banks, this is individual investors. This is institutions who do want to be invested in US assets. They’re comfortable being in corporate bonds. They’re comfortable clipping an extra percent and a half—

Kevin: But they don’t want Treasuries.

David: Right?

Kevin: So, it’s not just a central bank phenomenon. You’re saying private investors are coming out of Treasuries as well.

David: That’s right. And the US is not seen as a bad place to put capital. Quite the opposite. Again, equity and debt inflows, Q2, 4.49 trillion according to the Z.1 report. 3.27 trillion into equities. It’s not just sovereign wealth funds and central banks reducing their Treasury holdings. The Z.1 report I think was pretty critical on that point.

To what degree does gold capture capital flows over the next 6 to 12 months? I mean, honestly, we don’t know. But we’re concerned by this week and this year’s interest rate moves higher. Fed funds, which are merely catching up to what the bond market assumes is the new legitimate range, that’s already established. The bond market has spoken. This is where rates should be.

We talked about this a week ago. If we have any weakness in metals prices this week on the basis of: maybe he surprises with a 50 basis point increase.

Kevin: Buy some.

David: Boy, would the White House be ticked. I mean, he’s not a patriot. He’s a communist.

Kevin: Right.

David: He raised—

Kevin: It’s even worse.

David: Oh, it’s even worse.

The next move for us in the metals market is not ambiguous. The road ahead, we retake 5,000 an ounce and we press to new highs in 2027, 6,000, above. By 2030, eight to ten thousand an ounce.

Kevin: So, let me get this right. Back to 5,000, then on up. If the Republicans win, maybe we should be patriotic. If the Republicans win both the House and the Senate in November, you’re going to get 5,000 bucks. That’s what Trump told you.

David: I know.

Kevin: That’s just about the price of an ounce of gold.

David: Well, I should lock it in today because—

Kevin: We should send a flyer out and tell everybody to spend it on an ounce of gold.

David: Get your Trump dividend, buy an ounce of gold. By the time you’re paid the dividend, my guess is that it buys only a fraction of an ounce.

Kevin: Well, that’s true. You got to get that dividend real quick and then invest it.

David: Do you remember what happened with the COVID cash? Was that minorly inflationary or majorly inflationary?

Kevin: Yeah, it was inflationary, wasn’t it?

David: Fiscal stimulus— I mean, not that Congress is going to pass this. You don’t just send out $5,000 checks to everybody. This is a joke.

Kevin: Do you hear a sound in the background, Dave? What is the sound that you hear right now for that 5,000 per person?

David: Printing press. A printing press, yeah. I mean, we’re already running deficits of two trillion this year and he said, “We can afford it. We’re doing so well. We can send out another trillion.”

Kevin: What’s a little more?

David: Yeah, we’re going to make it three. We’re going to grow our way out. Bessent has a plan, 3% growth. We’ll get there. Not a problem. We got this covered.

Kevin: Well, vote Republican and get your rounds. I guess that’s what I should say.

David: Let’s do it.

*     *     *

Kevin: You’ve been listening to the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. I’m Kevin Orrick, along with David McAlvany. You can find us at McAlvany.com and you can call us at (800) 525-9556.

*     *     *

This has been the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. The views expressed should not be considered to be a solicitation or a recommendation for your investment portfolio. You should consult a professional financial advisor to assess your suitability for risk and investment. Join us again next week for a new edition of the McAlvany Weekly Commentary.

title.rendered: Markets Say Sweet, But Mood Sour At Home

content.rendered:
Podcast: Play in new window

  • Financial Conditions Have Not Been This Loose In 5 Years
  • Mag 7 Now Being Called The “Lag 7”
  • Dutch Government Wants Its Gold Repatriated From U.S. To London

Financial conditions are the loosest they have been in five years, risk markets remain comfortable, and investors are still borrowing aggressively to stay long. At home, the mood is very different as inflation, higher everyday costs, and strained household budgets keep consumer sentiment near recessionary levels. David McAlvany examines that growing disconnect, the rotation turning the Mag 7 into the “Lag 7,” and why most market risk indicators are still signaling smooth sailing. They also look at mounting pressure in global sovereign debt markets as governments face rising borrowing costs and record interest expenses. Finally, the Dutch government’s push to repatriate $12 billion in gold from the U.S. and Canada may be another sign that global trust is beginning to shift.

*     *     *

“I think when you look at the CNN Greed-Fear Index, it’s in the fear category. It’s not an extreme level. I don’t know. We could be putting in a market top. We have rotation of the Mag 7, recently referred to as the Lag 7, and that’s been going on for months. Now, we have a rotation out of semiconductors. Is this indicator suggesting that we’re starting a decline, but the worst is yet ahead? Again, where we get to extreme fear on the indicator? Extreme fear is not in the gauge yet.” —David McAlvany

*     *     *

Kevin: Welcome to the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. I’m Kevin Orrick along with David McAlvany.

Well, last week, Dave, you had your client call with the MWM clients, and I know a lot of them are coming in next month personally to see you. Isn’t it great that the team that you have and the clients that we have? What a blessing.

David: I must say, I think it’s extraordinary. The team that I get to work with, Ted and Robert, Philip Wortman, Morgan Lewis, I appreciate their integrity, hard work, intellectual curiosity. And the chemistry on the team is a lot of fun. So while we’re putting these quarterly calls together, I’m usually aware of what’s going to be said, and I’m always surprised at the same time. And I learn from these guys, which I love. I’ve got a lot of respect for them and I’m blessed to work with that extraordinary team.

Kevin: Isn’t it amazing that guys that are working for you and you’re taking notes while they’re talking?

David: Well, I’m equally blessed on the precious metal side of the business. The people are amazing. Kevin, come on. Our friendship has grown over a 30-year stretch, and our advisor team is filled with talented people. Our staff is off the charts. We’ve added six people to the team in the last several months, and I’m amazed by the caliber. Smart, hardworking, self-motivated, innovative. I mean, these are really great people. It’s an inspiring group to be a part of.

Kevin: You know what’s also amazing, though, Dave? We have these teams because we have amazing clients.

David: Yeah. To get to work with an amazing group of clients as well. As I get on calls with clients throughout the week, I realize that we have this relational nexus which is unreal. I’m naturally curious and love to learn, but add to that the motivation to serve our clients well, provide insight, guidance. I understand a lot of people wear themselves out during a career, and daily I’m inspired by the work and I’m inspired by the people.

Kevin: You’re talking about wearing yourself out and I still talk to Jim Deeds who’s in his 90s, and I think he wishes that he still was here, Dave. And I talk to other guys who were like, “Well, it’s maybe retirement age.” And then they question themselves. And I look at my weekend. Okay, I took Friday off and I was off Monday. I’m telling you what, I was ready to come back to work. You’re talking about you’re inspired. I love a little bit of time off. I don’t like a lot of time off. And it’s mainly because of the people we work with and for.

David: So it’s not too much time, too many honey-dos. I mean, it was Labor Day after all.

Kevin: It was. It was. Okay. Well, you caught me there. But yeah, I think I’d rather be calling my clients than fixing the refrigerator.

David: How’d that work for you?

Kevin: I got it fixed.

David: Nice. Nice.

Kevin: Two screws. That was all it took. So, yeah.

David: I have these miniature hero moments where I fix something and Mary-Catherine didn’t think I was capable of such a feat. I probably played up what the feat is, and it is two screws, but it was portrayed as an engineering masterpiece.

Kevin: Right, masterpiece. And you have to go find one of them and get the size exactly right. You have to act like it’s complex, a little bit like the financial markets. The financial markets are complex.

David: Well, they are complex.

Kevin: In a different way.

David: Yeah. There’s no pretending there. There’s so much complexity in the financial markets. It’s rare that you study all the factors in play and feel like you fully get it. And reflecting on a test I took when I was 25, the Johnson O’Connor, have we ever talked about the—

Kevin: That’s a personality—

David: Aptitude test.

Kevin: Aptitude test?

David: Yeah, not personality, aptitude, like, “What are you good at? What are you not good at? What is going to take more energy for you to do?”

Kevin: So repairing refrigerators with two small screws was not part of that?

David: No, not really. What it did show me is that I thrive with an investigative multidisciplinary synthesis of ideas leading to a defined course of action.

Kevin: Okay.

David: So diagnosis, prescription. It’s a combination of deep dive analysis with practical, actionable outcomes. And that’s my daily job.

Kevin: That’s amazing. That’s what you get to do. Yeah.

David: Yeah, it is amazing. Markets are rewarding, but again, the relational depth is even more so.

Kevin: Okay. So let’s do this today because a lot of times I hear our clients ask you, “Dave, what is it that you look for? What are some of the themes that you look for when you do some of that market analysis?” So why don’t we go through some of that right now and make it current?

David: Themes today, financial conditions, sentiment, and a few curious shifts in the bond and precious metals markets.

Kevin: Okay.

David: So, starting with financial conditions, the Chicago Fed publishes an index that measures money markets, bonds, stocks, shadow banking, suggestive of how tight or loose financial conditions are.

Kevin: Are we loose or tight right now financially?

David: And it’s called the Financial Conditions Index. Lo and behold, we have not been this loose since July 2021 during the meme stock melt-up, the everything bubble. So financial conditions are incredibly loose. And prior to 2021, you’d have to go back to the first quarter of 2014. This was several years after the European debt crisis. I wouldn’t say it was resolved, but you got to sort of paper over it with Mario Draghi’s “we’ll do whatever it takes” as he normalized yields and promised to use the full power of the European Central Bank to make sure that yields returned to normal.

Kevin: Yeah. And it was like a tidal wave of debt, and later inflation.

David: But yeah, financial conditions are loose today. And when conditions are loose, confidence is high. Investors are comfortable with risk, they’re aggressively investing, they’re speculating for growth. Now, you can flip the script when conditions tighten and risk comes out of the market. Then you’ve got caution which is pervasive, and you’ve got the mood of the market which sours.

Kevin: So they measure mood, though, don’t they? I mean, the Sentiment Index is a mood measurement device.

David: Yeah. There’s various measures of sentiment. I was comparing the index, this is the Financial Conditions Index. I was comparing that against the consumer sentiment numbers this week, so the University of Michigan numbers. Some interesting relationships were observable.

Normally, financial conditions lead and consumer sentiment shifts on a lagging basis. Consumer sentiment is more reflective of economic concern. So when you think about gasoline and food prices and inflation expectations, real wage growth, employment perceptions, fear of getting the pink slip, housing affordability or lack thereof—30 year fixed is at 6.71 this week.

Kevin: So what you’re talking about is the day-to-day grind, the day-to-day life. That’s what usually affects the mood.

David: These are the things that get factored in—more economic related—into the UMich number. This is what impacts people’s feelings about the economy. And they’re very different than credit spreads and other purely financial market metrics. But that lead/lag behavior is typical. We don’t have that right now. So that was one of the key observations. I’m looking at both of these charts.

Instead, what you see is consumer stress and concern while financial market largess is still significant and ramping. So the University of Michigan numbers earlier this year, they hit all time lows even while financial conditions remained super accommodative. They’re not at those all time lows, but they’re not far off them today. And, yes, financial conditions remain super accommodative. So the University of Michigan numbers are still at levels associated with recession, and you’d normally see a very sour equity market sentiment with the UMich numbers where they are.

Hardly the case today when you’re looking at risk assets. We don’t have anything circling the drain. In fact, everything’s like trees growing to the stars. There’s no limits. So the question on my mind, will we see the reverse lead/lag this time with economic concerns bleeding back into financial market conditions and a tightening there?

Kevin: Well, and so there is a disconnect with the mood though because with economic conditions, people right now are really feeling the pinch. Maybe their 401(k) or their investments are going up, but after listening to Jack Gamble last week talk to you about the AI bubble, I just wonder if that disconnect isn’t part of a shell game that’s going on with AI, and when that comes apart—if it comes apart, and it probably has to—that’s probably going to change. The financial conditions will shift to match the mood.

David: Yeah. The mood is strong because the narrative is strong.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: And so if people understand that it is more of a shell game and not something that is a layup, a guarantee, then yeah, you could definitely see sentiment shift and with it mood of the market. But again, I’m wondering if you’re not dealing with consumers who are so pinched at this point that it begins to have sort of a negative feedback loop into the financial markets, regardless of the AI stuff.

So we did take a deep dive down the AI rabbit hole, in part to look at the narrative driving so much of the current financial market enthusiasm. But growth in portfolio values on the back of equity outperformance, rampant debt expansion, modest premiums paid today in the marketplace for lower quality fixed income credit—all of that is at odds with the consumer’s perception, the present economic reality and what they anticipate in the near term, because University of Michigan has sort of an immediate sense—what’s your view here—and on the horizon—what’s your view out there—and they have two different measures. Both of those, the consumer’s not happy. The one dominant factor in the UMich numbers that stands out, not a surprise, inflation.

Kevin: Right. The price you pay at the store. Yeah.

David: High prices are creating pressure for household finances. So people feel one way about their budgets, this negative feelings, and they presently feel very differently about their portfolios, positive feelings, at least those who have portfolios to speak of.

Kevin: Right. And so if you don’t have a portfolio, you’re just feeling recession right now, right? But if you have a portfolio, it’s like, “Well, it’s costing us a lot at the store, but look what we’re making over in the stock market right now.”

David: So sentiment is the second topic. University of Michigan captures economic sentiment reasonably well, although there is certainly some partisan bias that shows up in the sampling. And it should come as no surprise that in an election year there are feelings and concerns which are more elevated. Inflation’s the dominant issue discussed by the respondents. Last week, that’s supported by the Institute for Supply Management Services and Manufacturing Indexes, particularly their prices paid components, both stronger than expected.

Kevin: So inflation in the source material basically.

David: It reinforces the fact that whether it’s services or manufacturing, input costs are remaining higher than they’d like them to be. And if they were hoping for lower numbers, they did not get them. So couple that with the Cleveland Fed’s interviews with local manufacturers dealing with some double digit increases in input costs—double digit—and this is an area that is unambiguously negative.

This won’t make its way into the CPI and PPI numbers this week. So we get those this week and we’ll have a catalyst for Warsh and company to do something or not do something. But again, what’s not going to get factored in, in addition to, I mean, we talked about ISM, we talked about consumer expectations, inflation expectations in the consumer numbers, but the Bloomberg Agricultural Spot Index, which tracks 10 major products, in August had its biggest monthly gains in more than a decade. And households can tell you about that. They can tell you a lot more than statisticians can.

Kevin: Yeah. And inflation is here. Now I’m wondering, and we can go back to this, but the bullishness right now in the market seems strong, but is there a way of measuring bullish and bearish, just what the sentiment is there on whether the market’s going to continue?

David: Yeah. There’s a bunch of different sentiment indicators. American Association of Individual Investors, the bull/bear spread, National Association of Active Investment Managers, the CNN Greed-Fear Index, Volatility Index, which we call VIX.

Kevin: And maybe even margin debt, right?

David: Margin debt. They’re all indicators of sentiment. So looking at the American Association of Individual Investors bull/bear spread, there’s only a two percentage point bullish bias, where you can see extremes in either direction 10 to 15 points apart. So if you look at the AAII numbers, it’s neutral.

Kevin: It’s like a room full of people that are sort of split in half right now.

David: Yeah. I forget what the exact number was. Maybe it’s 38, 36 and 20-odd in the middle, neutral, but it doesn’t tell you anything.

Kevin: Well, how about margin debt then?

David: Well, there’s actually the National Association of Active Investment Managers is a different look at margin. Not always, but it’s bullish enough to be net long the markets, 102%, almost 103% leveraged long position. So this is active managers who are saying we not only want to own the markets, but we’re willing to borrow—

Kevin: To own more.

David: Leverage the portfolio to own more.

Kevin: Well, we talked about AI again, that’s happening to a massive degree in AI. So they’re borrowing to buy more stocks.

David: Yeah. So you’ve got the professional investors who are at 103% market exposure, 102.6%. And then you’ve got margin debt, which is a better reflection of retail investors. And it came off the June all-time highs of 1.5 trillion. And it’s still near the record, 1.417 trillion. For perspective, that’s still 40% over last year’s levels.

Kevin: Wow.

David: So maybe it dropped 5% month over month, June to July—we don’t have the August figures yet—but it’s still 40%, almost 45% over last year’s levels. Those levels suggest manic confidence. And of course that’s what is supporting—one of the aspects of what’s supporting the current equities market. So sentiment, sentiment, sentiment. We’ve got a neutral reading. We’ve got a very bullish reading in the professional asset managers being net long 103, 102.6. We’ve got the margin numbers near all-time highs.

Kevin: But the economic mood is sour.

David: But the economic mood is sour. So that’s why I’m thinking about financial conditions versus how the households are feeling. And one of the things that I think this could set up is a nasty surprise in the midterm elections where Democrats sweep and now all of a sudden anybody who had any thought of a strong finish to the end of the year, low taxes going forward, you might be motivated to take some of those gains near the end of the fourth quarter and pay those cap gains taxes for year 2026 versus who the hell knows what you’re going to get in 2027 with a new congressional crowd.

Kevin: This weekend I was going through my pictures and I sent a picture. I went back to 2017 and sent a picture of you and your dad. After a full day of meeting with people in separate rooms, you had different clients coming in, and we were in Austin, and you guys were debriefing at the end of the day. I think about all the things that your dad used to tell us that the shift from greed to fear. Do you remember the story, the way your dad told it, about if you throw a bunch of Krugerrands, gold coins, out in the middle of the room and say, “Get what you can,” that’s greed. Everybody just jumps on. He says, “But if there was a nine-foot gorilla with a straight razor,” he always said the straight razor part, with a straight razor behind you, it’s going to turn to fear real quick.

And I’ve never forgotten that because panic is an interesting— We’re talking about sentiment and mood changes, but you don’t usually see gradual changes. What you see is something completely unexpected. The gorilla, the nine-foot gorilla, all of a sudden showing up, and it’s like, “Well, maybe he was always there. You just got greedy first.”

David: Well, and it shifts and then you figure out why it shifted after the fact, or at least that’s how the news media kind of tries to create some cause and effect to better understand it.

Kevin: They write books later. Yeah.

David: Here’s what caused this. If you spend any time underwater watching fish, it’s fascinating because they all move as a school, and none of the fish in the school know what’s happening. They just know what’s happening right next to them.

Kevin: You and I have gone diving and seen that where all of a sudden there’s just a change.

David: The whole school moves and they don’t know why. They just know that there’s movement and they have to respond. And then after the fact you can be like, “Oh, well, the tuna was getting ready to eat the one on the outer edge and he responded and it created this domino effect.” But the nature of the markets is to not know. And when sentiment shifts, then you can do sort of a postmortem and say, “Oh, well this is what happened.”

Kevin: But right now there’s no fear in the market.

David: There’s a little bit of fear, like you look at the CNN Greed-Fear Index. It was 64 a month ago. That was in the greed category. They kind of have it on an RPM spectrum. 64 was in the greed category, not the extreme greed category. Today it’s at 42. So it has crept into the fear category, nowhere near what you’d see with a market low. Market lows tap the extreme fear level. Market highs usually tap the extreme greed level. And I think with war uncertainty, there’s no doubt that’s a factor. We’ve got some concerns about the pressure from the oil markets and diesel and refined products. They haven’t gone away. We’ve got all-time highs in diesel. I rode my motorcycle to work. I mean, I can afford $7 a gallon. It just makes me angry. So I rode my bike.

Kevin: That is a big truck you drive when you’re not on the motorcycle, though. Yeah. You could pull a lot of horses with it, Dave. Let’s just put it that way.

David: Yeah. So I think when you look at the CNN Greed-Fear Index, it’s in the fear category. It’s not an extreme level. I don’t know. We could be putting in a market top. We have rotation of the Mag 7, recently referred to as the Lag 7.

Kevin: Isn’t that interesting?

David: Yeah.

Kevin: From Mag to Lag.

David: Yeah. And that’s been going on for months. Now we have a rotation out of semiconductors. Is this indicator suggesting that we’re starting a decline, but the worst is yet ahead? Again, where we get to extreme fear on the indicator? Extreme fear is not in the gauge yet.

Kevin: Okay. And one of the ways that you do measure, because we were talking today about what you analyze to look at on a consistent basis, volatility is often a sign of things shifting, the volatility index.

David: And yet you have nothing there. It’s not giving you any indication. VIX is often thought of as a market sentiment gauge as well. It’s a ratio between puts and calls. It’s indicative of hedging market risk and anticipated future volatility in the S&P 500. Last week we hit a multi-month low at 14. Zero alarm bells there. Quite the opposite. It’s basically saying everything’s good. There is nothing to worry about here.

So these indicators are not consistent with the economic sentiment. So you’ve got financial market indicators which are a form of financial market sentiment largely positive to neutral, and then the sentiment indicators tied more to the economy decidedly negative. And this is the question, right? Does one lead this time differently than it usually does? The economic side usually lags. It may be leading this time.

Kevin: For the first time in my life, I read Jekyll and Hyde. I don’t know who sent it to me, but somebody I talked to said you ought to read this, and sent it to me. It’s amazing how you can have two personalities. Beautifully written. Robert Louis Stevenson wrote that book, but it really was challenging to me because it’s like, wow, how many areas in my own life is there a Jekyll and Hyde thing going on where there’s an inconsistency with maybe the outside world or even an inconsistency within myself? What you’re telling me right now, Dave, is maybe what we have is an inconsistency where the financial markets have a life of their own, call it a day night, or a day life, or a nightlife, whatever it is. And it’s not matching the economic mood, what it actually takes to survive.

I think about debt, Dave. We’ve been talking about equities and volatility and that type of thing, but when people are fearful, they demand more on what they loan. So the difference between US Treasuries, which supposedly are very safe, or like corporate bonds, a lot of times you’ll have a pretty large spread there because the fear is that the corporation might default.

David: That’s another measure of sentiment. It’s like a thermometer, if you will. 98.6, no big deal. 99.6, no big deal under certain conditions. 101, everyone’s paying attention. It’s a mild fever. 104, you should probably see a doctor. 105 or 106, you’re probably in the ER. So the thermometer gives you a gauge for “don’t worry” to, “oh, definitely panic.”

Kevin: Right. So yields, right?

David: High yield, whether it’s credit default swaps or high yield credit spreads, they’re telling you that within the fixed income markets, in the debt markets. High yield credit spreads are more of a measure of institutional risk concerns. So we’ve talked about individual investors, we’ve talked about margin debt, we’ve talked about professional money managers. In this case, this is really just institutions that are concerned about high yield credit spreads. When the gap between Treasuries and bond yields is wide spread, risk awareness is high and credit concerns are being priced in. You’re going to pay for it.

Kevin: Right.

David: Right. So again, temperatures are rising. When the gap between them is narrow, credit risk is not priced in. Concerns are low. So like VIX, credit spreads right now are suggestive of good times. Credit spreads are super narrow. No alarm bells.

Kevin: This is like having a low volatility index, and there’s not much in the way of credit spreads.

David: Zero concern.

Kevin: This is smooth sailing, Dave.

David: It’s smooth sailing.

Kevin: What are you worried about?

David: Issuance of high yield debt higher this year than last year by 21% year to date compared to last year, I think 256, almost 257 billion in issuance.

Kevin: Right.

David: It’s interesting. So maybe we should just say, “Hey, there’s not going to be any issues at all. That’s what the market is telling us.”

Kevin: Right. But the market also offers instruments that allow you to insure against a major change, right?

David: Right. And those would also suggest there’s no concerns. I mean, this is flood insurance.

Kevin: The credit default swaps.

David: People are buying flood insurance in the middle of a drought.

Kevin: Right.

David: They’re getting it for free.

Kevin: Okay.

David: So credit default swaps, like an insurance policy on a bond default, pricing for CDS, credit default swaps, similar to credit spreads, indicative when and if institutional players are concerned about fixed income markets. So investment grade, CDS traded below 50 basis points last week, in line with the lows that we saw in 2020 and in line with the pre-COVID lows of 44 basis points, which marked the low going back to the global financial crisis. So again, that’s pre-COVID, in between the global financial crisis and COVID, that cyclical trough, 44 bips. We were within a stone’s throw of that last week. So no concerns marked in that market.

Kevin: Right. Okay. So you have simplified for the listeners through the years one thing in particular, and that is the cost of money. I joke with you about reading long books about interest rates, but when you have available money, liquidity, it seems that you have this smooth sailing like in the financial markets. So right now, liquidity must be available, Dave.

David: Yeah. Have a lot, costs a little. Have a little, cost a lot.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: And there is a lot. How available is capital and at what price? These are considerations that start in the financial sphere and can ultimately bleed into the economy. What we can say is that capital is very available at present. Okay. I just mentioned the 256 billion in high yield junk debt. Now the contrast, of course, is that the cost of government debt is gradually rising. And frankly, the cost of capital is rising everywhere, just without credit risk differentiation. So the spreads are staying constant as everything gets pushed up, but you’re not getting a bump in government debt and a spike in investment grade or high yield or what have you. So the fact that no radical repricing has occurred, it’s very helpful for the issuers. And with it being helpful for the issuers, they’re tapping the markets for hundreds of billions of dollars.

Now for creditors or for investors, it’s perhaps the gradual boiling of the frog scenario versus the scalding water creating that volatile reaction. But there’s nothing crazy happening in the debt markets today. What is a little crazy— I take that back. There’s two crazy things. We’ll get to it. What is a little crazy is that we’re on track for record-breaking issuance of zero-coupon convertible debt.

Kevin: You mentioned that in the meeting. Why don’t you explain again what a zero-coupon bond is basically?

David: Yeah. Zeros are debt instruments that don’t have an actual interest payment. It has an implied or phantom payment attached to it. So you can buy that instrument at a discount and they’re not paying you anything, but it matures at par, or it’s supposed to mature at par.

Kevin: So it’s a type of interest, but you buy it at a discount and then the assumption is that it’s going to mature at par or whatever they can pay, right?

David: Mature at par or convert to company equity.

Kevin: Okay.

David: In the case of a zero-coupon convertible, they don’t have to give you your money back. They can give you—

Kevin: You can become a shareholder.

David: Yeah. I mean, think about a zero-coupon convertible bond and try to imagine what it was like to be in Cyprus or Greece when your deposit was converted to a position in bank shares. And that was considered a disaster because you had a debt instrument and you were getting income, and then overnight you’re an equity owner in a—

Kevin: They named that bail-in. Remember that? It’s the difference between a bailout— A bail-in is when everybody just becomes a shareholder.

David: They’re not exactly the same, but there’s enough similarities to realize that how someone is sold a product absolutely matters. And obviously the zero-coupon convertible debt is not being sold as a bail-in, but it sure feels like that’s what it is in the end. What are you going to get at the end of this?

Kevin: Well, think about it. Okay, put yourself in the position of when you were a kid and you’d put a quarter in and they’d sell super balls or gumballs or whatever. But what they’re basically saying is, if you don’t get a gumball or a super ball, you get a portion of the share of the gumball machine. Now granted, it’s empty, but you get to be a shareholder of the gumball machine. Yeah.

David: Well, so 186.8 billion in global issuance of zero-coupon convertible bonds year to date. 60% of those bonds are related to AI, according to Axios. And last week Nvidia invested 3.5 billion in zero-coupon bonds from a Taiwanese chip maker. So again, Nvidia is investing in lots of different things to get a lot of capital to do that.

Kevin: We heard that last week.

David: The recycling, the incestuous nature of their capital spending, is worth keeping in mind. But here it is, they have an appetite for zero-coupon convertible bonds too. They want to own a piece of the action in Taiwanese chip makers. Who doesn’t these days?

Kevin: Let me just translate before we move to precious metals because a lot of our listeners, they’re wanting to know what your thought is there. But what I’m hearing in this show is that the financial markets have plenty of liquidity.

David: Yup.

Kevin: Very little fear.

David: No.

Kevin: Smooth sailing right now, and yet the person at home, okay, so I get home and my wife’s like, “You wouldn’t believe what I spent at the store. And do we really have to fill the car up again?” It’s over a hundred bucks to fill the car up. And we’re blessed because I have an income and yes, we can do that, but there’s two—Jekyll and Hyde—going on right now at the same time. And what’s interesting is that character lived perfectly fine with both of those in tandem for a period of time, and then that separation caught up with him.

David: Yep.

Kevin: Yep.

David: So the second crazy thing I was going to talk about, we’ve got bonds, precious metals. Those are two areas I want to wrap up with. We’ve said there’s no drama playing out in the bond markets except with government bonds. And it is a global phenomenon where rates are increasing for sovereigns, taking out multi-decade highs. It’s across Europe, it’s across Asia, it’s across the US. 10-year rates, 4.78 here in the US, 30-year debt, five and a quarter, which compares to the UK at 5.15 and 5.79 for their 30-year paper. That’s now higher than during the Liz Truss bond panic in 2022. Now note, there’s not a panic in sovereign debt, but there is pressure in the sovereign debt markets. And that pressure has already brought us to the point of the maximum level of concern in the 2022 Liz Truss panic. Sentiment is fine. Pricing has already shifted.

Kevin: But the governments are having to pay a little bit more to borrow money.

David: Yeah.

Kevin: Across the board.

David: Or in some cases a lot more. I mean, roll the clock back just a few years ago and the Japanese weren’t paying anything.

Kevin: Do you remember those days, Dave? Negative interest rates. We had several years of shows where we were scratching our heads going, “How does this work?”

David: And then not just in Japan.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: So 2.88 for the 10-year in Japan, 3.94, up from zero just a few years ago. Germany’s at 3.36 and 3.82, 3.82% on their 30-year paper. So fiscal pressures are growing, which is also a global phenomenon. So I’m not just picking on the US. We have our own issues, but they’re just not unique anymore. More money is spent on debt service than defense in the UK, in France, in the US.

Kevin: As of last year.

David: And at least a dozen other OECD countries. These are your developed world rich countries. At least a dozen plus those. We’re talking 12 to 15 companies that are paying more in interest than on defense.

Kevin: Countries. Countries, not companies, right?

David: Countries.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: Did I say companies?

Kevin: You said companies, but that’s okay.

David: I meant countries. Thank you.

Kevin: Because it fits in, Dave, because Nvidia is also doing the same type of thing.

David: Right. Well, the OECD countries are this year going to borrow an additional $18 trillion between them.

Kevin: Wow.

David: So bad habits die hard, and they’re not even trying to curb a bad habit. 18 trillion between the OECD countries, that’s new debt for this year, according to the Financial Times, combined interest expense over two trillion. And that’s for the first time ever, over two trillion in aggregate for those OECD countries. Of course, the US stands out with 1.25 trillion of that already paid year to date. The UK is spending one in 10 pounds of tax revenue on interest. We’re spending one in five.

Kevin: And you know what? We’d be spending more than that if we weren’t buying our own bonds.

David: So think about this. Trump is like, “We should have lower rates. Our house is totally in order.”

Kevin: It’s not patriotic if you raise rates. That’s what he said.

David: The UK is paying higher rates than we are, and yet they’re spending 10% of their revenue.

Kevin: And we’re 20.

David: And we’re close to 20. So whose house is in order? Let’s not kid ourselves.

Kevin: Right. But Bessent has been buying back our Treasuries.

David: Last week—

Kevin: Okay. To keep that interest rate looking good.

David: Last week, 12 and a half billion US debt. Talk about circular financing. It’s a little bit different than Nvidia, but it’s still just gamesmanship and shell games. Buying down the rate, short end of the curve, not sure why he’s doing that. 2026 to 2028 maturities. We noted last year that Mike Wilson was bearish on debt. This is the CIO at Morgan Stanley. And he recommended replacing half of your fixed income allocation in a model portfolio with gold. He sees, as we do, that there’s considerable ongoing impairment in the bond market. I guess what I’m trying to illustrate is that it’s starting with the sovereign debt markets. That doesn’t mean it can’t migrate elsewhere, but today at least, it’s contained, and there are no indications in those financial market indicators suggesting that it’s migrating yet. So—

Kevin: Do you remember a few years ago, Dave? So you’re talking about Morgan Stanley replacing it with gold. One of the things that strikes me right now is how many people are bringing their gold home. Do you remember a few years ago when Germany said, “Hey, we would like one-fifth of our gold sent from the United States to Germany.” And the initial reaction from the US was, “Well, yeah, we’ll be happy to do that over the next seven years.”

David: It was interesting. It was like, “What’s the delay?”

Kevin: Why?

David: Just order up a truck, a plane, a boat? This is not a big deal.

Kevin: Unless have you been leasing it out to somebody else? I don’t know.

David: I don’t know.

Kevin: I don’t know. But other people are doing that, too.

David: Because the logistics are pretty easy. Moving product’s pretty easy.

Kevin: We saw that earlier this year when they loaded 747s up with silver.

David: Right.

Kevin: Yeah.

David: So I know it’s a news cycle coincidence, but both headlines are indicative of a different kind of sentiment shift. You’ve got the Dutch Central Bank repatriating 12 billion in gold from US and Canadian vaults.

Kevin: So they’re doing the same thing that the Germans did.

David: Same thing.

Kevin: Bring it back.

David: They want it closer to home. London’s good enough. And they’re citing geopolitical concerns. Okay. Well, I mean, I think that’s a diplomatic way of saying we’re losing trust and confidence with the US, the US Treasury, US foreign policy, US foreign policy overreach, and we feel better working with the Brits, and we feel better having it closer at hand. And the US, not only in its confiscation of assets from Russia in 2022, is now running sort of a reputation of overreach. And this is a European Union player. This is a different lens through which you could look at sentiment. There is a shift there. We don’t really trust you guys. We’re not going to say that. We’re going to say it’s geopolitical risk that is a concern for us.

Kevin: Well, we’re not talking man in the street right now. What we’re talking about are the decisionmakers at the very top.

David: Yeah. And then last week came the announcement of the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund cutting fixed income allocations to sovereign debt from 70% to 50% in their bond portfolio.

Kevin: So they’re concerned about sovereign debt as well.

David: They’re concerned about sovereign debt, not necessarily US debt in general, but sovereign debt in particular. And so there’ll be some recycling into corporate credit, into mortgage-backed securities, into other things.

Kevin: Yeah, but how much does that affect Treasuries? Because Japan has been also reducing their Treasury hold.

David: This is just from— Because you’re talking about a $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund. This is a reduction in US Treasuries by $80 billion.

Kevin: Wow. That’s significant.

David: It is significant. That’s 80 billion in liquidations of US Treasuries out of the total of 106 billion, and that captures all of their sovereign debt exposure as they reduce it from a 70% allocation within the fixed income bond index to 50%. 2.3 trillion in assets, they’re not moving from fixed income to gold. So this is not a replay of like a Mike Wilson thing. It’s fixed income to fixed income. They’re just looking for a little bit more yield.

Kevin: But that means Bessent’s probably going to have to come in and buy some of that, too. It’s not like we have people lined up at the door to buy Treasuries right now.

David: No, I think the Norwegians move out of government paper, it’s an important signpost.

Kevin: Right. So the Netherlands are bringing their gold home. The Norwegians, which sometimes, we get confused. They both start with an N.

David: Are saying, “You can have your paper back.”

Kevin: Yeah, you can have your paper back. Wow.

David: This week, assuming a stronger CPI print, Warsh would then have permission to raise rates 25 basis points. An initial negative reaction to the gold market, I think that’d be normal. Consider where gold is likely to be over the next one- to two-year time frame. I kind of hope that gold takes a hit this week. We’re on a path to 8,000 to 10,000 an ounce. That is a path that’s easier to imagine by the day when you look at the pressures in the global government bond market.

And so I would recommend using any weakness prior to 2027 as an opportunity to add ounces, add ounces, add ounces as often as you can and as often as you get a break in price. So while the markets are enamored today with risk assets, there is going to come a day when risk indicators, instead of where they’re at today, like we discussed earlier, they will be sounding an alarm. And the day that the risk indicators—which today are flat and saying nothing of concern is on the horizon, nothing to worry about here, move along, have fun speculating—when those alarm bells are going off, the gold available for purchase is going to be very limited. And that’s the context where you have soaring prices reflective of a demand wave we haven’t seen from the investing public in more than a generation.

Kevin: Right. Even the last, the rise that we’ve had so far has been non-public participatory.

David: Central bank-driven. By the way, World Gold Council numbers on central bank gold consumption continue to be strong. Most recent monthly totals out of China, 20 tons for the month, and that’s their 21st consecutive month of purchases.

There’s people who get it and people who don’t. And as we talk today about sentiment indicators, maybe the folks who are super positive about where AI is going, super positive about credit concerns, maybe they’re onto something. If they’re not, again, this is where you’ve got so many people loaded on one side of the boat, when they decide to move en masse, it’s going to get very interesting.

Kevin: You’d better buy gold.

David: I hope you own what you need long before that day arrives.

*     *     *

Kevin: You’ve been listening to the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. I’m Kevin Orrick along with David McAlvany. You can find us at mcalvany.com and you can call us at 800-525-9556.

*     *     *

This has been the McAlvany Weekly Commentary. The views expressed should not be considered to be a solicitation or a recommendation for your investment portfolio. You should consult a professional financial advisor to assess your suitability for risk and investment. Join us again next week for a new edition of the McAlvany Weekly Commentary.

title.rendered: The AI Bubble’s Circular Financing Problem with Jack Gamble

content.rendered:
Podcast: Play in new window

Jack Gamble of @NobodySpecialFinance joins David McAlvany to follow the money behind the AI boom. Jack examines the circular financing connecting Nvidia, CoreWeave, OpenAI, Microsoft, and others, along with massive data center spending, GPU depreciation, mounting debt, and the constant need for new capital. AI may prove transformative, but does that mean today’s investments will prove profitable? Jack and David explore the financial risks beneath the AI boom.

“AI is inflationary at this point in time, highly inflationary. And what Secretary Bessent is doing in suppressing yield, that is delaying the inevitable comeuppance that would kill this bubble. All these things we’re doing to keep interest rates from rising, as they naturally need and must be allowed to do in order to restore a healthy economy, artificially suppressing that is prolonging this bubble, which is making the inevitable result of it that much worse.” —Jack Gamble

*     *     *

Kevin: Welcome to the McAlvany Weekly Commentary.

Dave, today’s an unusual day because we’re interviewing somebody who calls himself nobody special. And when I heard that, I thought, well, then why are we entering into a conversation with nobody special? But I’ll tell you what, this guy is special, isn’t he?

David: Well, you follow the truth where it takes you. And sometimes for us, that’s into economic tomes and things that nobody reads or hasn’t read for 20 years, but should have some familiarity with. That could be economic theories or conceptions which have been left behind, whether it’s the efficient market hypothesis or—

We look at things critically. When I came across Jack Gamble and the Nobody Special podcast, I thought, he’s doing good work and he’s got the mental chops to go deep, partially because he’s trained his mind to do so. When you spend a couple years in nuclear engineering as a mechanical engineer, you start asking questions and you have to find the answer. And like a dog on the hunt, once he’s discovered something, he goes deep, and I appreciate that. So I wanted to bring him into the conversation for the McAlvany Weekly Commentary.

Kevin: One of the things that I enjoyed when I first came to work here was the ideology of your dad. When your dad would see something that other people needed to know, he was on it, and he just made sure that other people knew. And Jack is like that. Jack is driven, even if it’s at a risk to himself, he’s driven to get good information to the people. And what he’s seeing right now needs to be explained.

David: Yeah, the AI bubble has some complexity to it and that’s what we’re going to dig into today.

Jack Gamble, great to have you on. Host of the Nobody Special podcast. Mechanical engineer, curious, critical in your appraisal of Wall Street and structured finance. You bring that to your audience on a daily basis. And we’re interested in the sleuthing that you’ve done on AI, what without a doubt is the greatest equity bubble of all time. Today we want to explore accounting gimmickry. We want to explore vendor financing, round tripping of revenue.

Let’s start with some context. The everything bubble ended in the fourth quarter of 2021. Maybe we can dive in on the AI narrative taking root in 2022, perhaps even the backstory, the DeepMind paper from 2027, just to set the context for what this bubble is, how it’s been building, and how it’s, I guess you could say degrading as time progresses.

Jack: Yeah, that’s a really good intro, and it’s the perfect place to start with the AI bubble or the AI mania, as I call it, that Google DeepMind paper, it was called “Attention is All You Need.” That came out in 2017. And that’s where the large language model was basically invented, in that white paper, or the transformer they called it. It was a mathematical model for predicting the importance of a word in a string of text. And when they fed this thing a certain amount of data and it came back with the outputs, they realized this is almost like talking to a person. Almost. It wasn’t quite as good. And so the theory was, if we scale this, if we give it more data and more computing power, maybe we can make this as smart as a person. And then, as you mentioned, the end of the everything bubble, right?

We all lived through the vid in 2020 and then we go through this period of easy money, the stimi cash gets flowing, and then that comes to an abrupt end. At the end of 2021, they announced that the Fed is going to start tapering their purchases, tapering their QE, and then tightening is right around the corner.

It very predictably led to a bear market in tech especially in 2022. And so the tech industry needed that shiny new thing. The crypto thing was played out, the internet of things was played out, Web3 was played out. They needed something to get that hype train going again.

The world was still awash with trillions of dollars in excess capital. The reverse repo was full at the time. And so there was money ready to go to work. And it really looks like in late 2022, they launched ChatGPT, much to the surprise of the board of directors at OpenAI, who found out after Sam Altman had launched the product.

It looks like they fired off this experiment to take the Google white paper and give it all the information they could steal, and finance this experiment with all the compute they could possibly give it, financed by what I now believe is the biggest accounting fraud in human history, the AI bubble. And we’re now four years into that. And as we’ll get into over the next few minutes, we are yet to produce a single penny of profit, and there are yet to be any observable gains in productivity despite increasingly ridiculous science fiction derivative hype talking points from the people who are pushing this experiment.

David: We’ve had CapEx booms in the past, and maybe the most recent was the tech bubble. You could certainly go back in time and look at the building out of the railroads. And without a doubt, the notion that these were revolutionary proved to be true. So it’s not a concern, I think on my part or your part, that AI is here to stay or it has transformative impact to the markets and to how we do life in the future. But it’s a question of how you finance it and what is involved. I think about rails, they don’t really go out of style and they have a pretty decent shelf life. You build them and they’re there for a hundred years or more. In this case, you’re talking about GPU life cycles that don’t really have a hundred-year stretch ahead of them. So this massive CapEx spend, maybe you can talk a little bit about the shortsightedness of what we’re spending and what we actually get for it.

Jack: And those are two great comparisons, the railroad bubble and the telecom, the dot.com bubble, because in both of those instances, you did have a very revolutionary new technology that was very useful. All the companies that borrowed too much and spent too much to develop excess capacity that wasn’t needed went bankrupt, but eventually that capacity was utilized. It was sold for pennies on the dollars when the debt went bad, the empty tracks, the dark fiber, it became known as all the cable that they laid in the telecom. Eventually the market grew into that, and so it produced value over time. That’s not going to happen with the AI bubble. This equipment that we’re building, these data centers that we’re building, has a very short useful life and an incredibly short obsolescence cycle. My friend Ed Zitron and even Michael Burry of Big Short fame have both drawn a lot of attention to the depreciation bomb that is about to go off in the AI space.

Today’s CapEx is tomorrow’s depreciation. A lot of that depreciation hasn’t even started yet. There’s an accounting gimmick called construction in progress where, as long as the data center hasn’t been switched on yet, it’s still being built, and therefore we don’t have to start depreciating the asset. And you’ve got more data centers in construction and progress right now than you actually have operating.

And so, much of the CapEx that has already been spent on GPUs that are still sitting in warehouses because it’s meant for data centers that haven’t been built yet, that depreciation clock hasn’t even started. And then once you do throw the switch, it’s debatable how long these GPUs are going to last. Some say three years, some go as long as seven to 10. It won’t matter because, besides the fact that these GPUs and these data centers are going to depreciate dramatically once you turn them on, and besides the fact that, yeah, AI is not going away—the market will use AI like it used the train, like it used the dot-coms, but it won’t be using data centers.

AI usage, in particular inference, which is the use of an AI model after it’s trained, that’s going to go local. We’ll still be using the big data centers for training the frontier models. You need the most current equipment, big cluster of it to create the model in the first place. That’s training. But training is only 10 to 30% of the demand for these compute clusters at data centers. Most of the demand, some estimates vary from 70 to 90%. Most of it is inference, the actual use of the product after it’s created. And inference is increasingly going local, especially after the token maxing phenomenon we saw at the beginning of this year when a lot of tech companies were telling employees “use it as much as possible.” And then OpenAI and Anthropic switch over to token-based billing because they were trying to clean up their books before their IPOs.

And these companies got their bills for the tokens, and said, “Whoa, everybody stop. Stop token maxing.” And Anthropic and OpenAI were like, “Look at our revenue growth,” never mind the fact that it’s about to plateau because everybody stopped token maxing. And now people are starting to be more choosy about how they use these tokens. You’ve also got pricing pressure from Chinese knockoffs are starting to suppress the price of these tokens, making them cheaper, driving these companies further into the red. And you’ve also got, people have figured out that you can run these things on local hardware.

You can take a distilled model that is 85 to 90% as good as the frontier products, and you can run it on a Mac mini in your house, a Mac mini that might cost you 800 or $900, and you never have to go to a data center for anything, not a single token. It runs locally. And even better, all your data, all your intellectual property, everything is staying where you control it. It’s not going out to the cloud where it can be used to train a chatbot to replace you someday.

And so, I think certainly for most consumer applications, for any business application where data security is important, which is a lot of them, certainly healthcare, legal, I think the future of AI is on local equipment, not cloud, which means these data centers that are being built will be useless in a couple of years, probably sooner.

David: Well, Jack, I’m just picturing Kevin Costner and the Field of Dreams and this notion that if you build it, they will come. And we’ve got Louisiana, Kentucky, Virginia, so many states that are doing just that. Massive deals, massive tax savings, communities are tripping over themselves to offer incentives to build something that they assume will be transformative. If you build it, they will come. So you’ve hit on one particular weakness.

There’s this other issue of, in the early phase of a bubble you get equity investors on board, and in the early stages maybe you’ve got reasonable value on the table. But as the equity of particular companies increases, now all of a sudden you’re paying a lot for a little. You’re not paying a little for a lot, you’re paying a lot for a little. Then in the later stages you’ve got debt and the need for financing even more growth.

The GPU life cycle is one issue which is sort of a critical risk. Talk to us about debt and how these companies are utilizing debt, and maybe some of the implied or the future tense weakness of that structure.

Jack: Yeah. So this is very important for people to realize, because something changed in just the last few months. The hyperscalers, which are your Mag Seven companies, your big guys, your Googles, Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, their free cash flow has gone negative, almost all of them. Only Microsoft still has significant positive free cash flow, which means their money in the bank is going down. So they can no longer finance this build-out with their other businesses. Microsoft is the only one that makes enough money off of Windows and Office to be able to finance building more data centers. All the rest of them are having to take out debt. And of course, that debt is expensive as interest rates are rising. Everybody’s in the press today talking about rising interest rates.

And so they’re now turning to private credit. Private credit is an industry that has spent the last nine months telling its investors, no, you can’t have your money back, because the assets on their books are not worth what they tell people they are. And so now these private credit companies are being loaded up with data center debt. And Microsoft and Meta and Amazon are not reporting this debt that they’re taking out on their books. They’re using what’s called special purpose vehicles, which anybody who’s around for Enron knows a lot about special purpose vehicles.

It’s when you create a shell of a company for a single project that you’re working on, and then that asset and the debt that pays for it lives on that shell company’s balance sheet, not yours. And so you don’t report it to your investors. You go look at Meta’s balance sheet, you can’t see all the debt they’re borrowing to build that giant data center in Louisiana that they partnered with Blue Owl to build, which Blue Owl is the poster child for the blow-up in private credit these days. And so these private credit facilities are now being used to pay for it.

NVIDIA came out just about a month ago now, I guess, with what I consider one of the most grotesque displays of moral hazard I’ve ever seen, when Jensen Huang and the private credit executives sat around the table at CNBC and congratulated themselves on how they were going to continue to finance this experiment with people’s pensions, IRAs, and 401Ks. This debt is being parked into highly complex, very difficult to see through financial instruments, asset backed securities, and it’s being sold to bond funds. And it’s being aided by the fact that in a lot of cases, NVIDIA themselves is backstopping this debt, providing credit guarantees.

And so, even though these companies are all destined to lose money on these investments, again, they’re yet to produce their first penny of profit, and they’re all deeply indebted, they’re being given investment grade credit ratings by the rating agencies because NVIDIA’s attached. They’re using NVIDIA’s name as a credit wrapper to make these projects look less risky. Again, it’s all being sold to people’s retirement accounts. I think most people are in something like a 60/40 portfolio in their IRA or their 401K. Their guy probably told them it’s nice and diversified, 60% stocks, 40% bonds. That 60% stocks is now almost entirely tied to the AI bubble.

The Mag Seven companies alone are 35% of the S&P 500 now, and that’s just the Mag Seven. You’ve also got utility stocks, Caterpillar, John Deere, GE Vernova, Eaton, 3M, Corning. All of these companies are now trading like AI companies. I mean, John Deere, their biggest growth sector is selling generators to data centers right now. Since when is John Deere an AI company? That is how big this bubble has gotten. It’s now swallowing up everything.

So the 60 in your 60/40 portfolio is already entirely dependent on these AI stocks, whether you realize it or not. But now they’re coming for the 40. Now they’re coming for the bonds, and they’re using private credit to do it. They’re getting investment ratings so they can sell it to these bond funds that are in people’s retirement accounts.

I don’t think the risk on them is being adequately measured and reported to people. And so people who think they’re diversified because they trust their guy to spread them out don’t realize it is one crowded-as-hell trade and everybody is now in it. Anybody with a retirement account is now in this trade.

David: Well, the concentration risk is pretty interesting. Particularly you look at it from a historical perspective, past CapEx booms have exhibited the same thing. 40% of market cap is usually the peak. There’s only one exception to that. And you have to go back to the railroads where frankly there weren’t that many companies listed in the mid to late 1800s. So it got as high as 60% in terms of the rails concentration.

But you look at more recent CapEx booms, and 40% as an expression of stock market capitalization, that kind of concentration is its own version of danger. And so you talked about 35% just in the Mag Seven, and then you expanded that list to other names which are participating on an ancillary basis. And we’re already there at the 40% and probably not going to see 60. But it is an indication, it is a signal that you’re at the end of a cycle, not at the beginning when you begin to see that concentration.

What do you think about Trump’s executive order allowing for alternative investments into 401ks? You talk about the 60/40 mix and investors not knowing that they’re participating because they’re not necessarily going out and buying Nvidia.
